articles.title_orig: China's growth accelerates as AI export boom outweighs domestic weakness
articles.title_zh: China's growth accelerates as AI export boom outweighs domestic weakness
articles.content_orig:
China's economic growth picked up in the three months to the end of September, rebounding from a three-year low as the artificial intelligence (AI) boom helped boost exports.
The world's second largest economy grew by 4.5% in the third quarter, up from the previous period but below the 5% expansion recorded from January to March, according to official Chinese data.
The latest figure is at the bottom end of Beijing's annual growth target of 4.5%-5%, which analysts have said gives policymakers room to address the country's economic challenges.
While exports have helped offset weak spending at home, global trade tensions and uncertainty over AI investments are clouding its outlook.
China's National Bureau of Statistics said on Monday that the economy "sustained steady development against pressure" and showed "momentum with new growth drivers and improving structure".
With exports climbing, China's trade surplus - the amount of goods and services it sells abroad compared to what it buys from other countries - is on track to overtake the record $1.2tn (£900bn) seen last year.
Sales of high-tech goods rose by 14.3% while the production of both batteries and industrial robots grew by more than 29%, official figures showed.
Oxford Economics researcher Sheana Yue said manufacturing and high-tech exports have boosted China's growth, despite weak investment and domestic spending.
But property investment fell by more than 20% in the first nine months from the same period last year, official data also showed.
China's economy has struggling to shake off a long-running property slump, after years of overbuilding and excessive borrowing by private developers.
There are still no signs that this trend will end soon, Yue said.
Trade uncertainties and geopolitical issues have also made Chinese consumers more "pessimistic" and unwilling to spend, she added.
The effects of Beijing's targeted support measures for businesses have yet to be seen, said Dave Chia, an economist at Moody's Analytics.
Several risks stand out from the data, including China's reliance on a "single external engine" in exports, he added.
The technology industry has been a key driver of China's growth in recent quarters.
Global demand for computer chips and other components used to build AI data centres has helped to ease pressure on Beijing and cushion the impact of sluggish domestic consumption.
Chinese businesses have leaned heavily on exports as a prolonged property slump, weak wage growth and high youth unemployment have weighed on consumer spending at home.
In September, Beijing unveiled a raft of support measures, including lower interest rates for some businesses and subsidies for property buyers, in an effort to boost the economy.
But Beijing is facing a backlash from Western economies - including the US and European Union - as manufacturers struggle to compete with large amounts of cheap Chinese goods.
There are also concerns over the billions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure and whether the companies making those investments can deliver on their promises of generating huge profits.

articles.title_orig: Macron calls for calm in France and warns rioting must not escalate
articles.title_zh: Macron calls for calm in France and warns rioting must not escalate
articles.content_orig:
French President Emmanuel Macron has called for "calm and order" after a major day of protests turned into rioting and looting on Saturday, and as some disorder continued in Paris on Sunday.
In a national address from the Élysée Palace, he warned those who had taken part not to "escalate", adding: "We all feel anger and shame."
Some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets for largely peaceful protests against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.
Macron said a distinction must be drawn between the "legitimate demands" of protesters and "those who destroyed, smashed and looted".
Police have arrested about 2,400 people, according to France's interior ministry.
The French president said "nothing justifies" the "unbridled" violence seen and said those involved would face justice.
Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, also came out in Paris, Marseille and other towns and cities, with some setting fire to cars and buildings.
Following some of the worst scenes of public disorder in modern French history, France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu will on Monday hold a crisis cabinet meeting .
On Sunday, looting and clashes with police continued on a smaller scale in parts of the capital and Lyon.
Tear gas and stun grenades were fired at hundreds of people in Paris, according to the AFP news agency, and bottles and rocks were again hurled at police.
Sunday saw cities across the country confront the impact of what developed into one of the worst bouts of disorder in modern French history.
In Limoges, the ornate 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire started by rioters on Saturday, its clock tower and roof collapsing and the flames took hold.
Speaking near the ruined building, Annèyse said: "This is very upsetting. Harming heritage buildings just because you are angry at the government is selfish, I think. It's hurting everybody."
"It's awful and unbelievable," said another man who gave his name as Gerrard. "We are very sad and I think it will be a long time to put it back as it was before."
Shopkeepers were seen early on Sunday morning picking up large shards of glass in Paris as rubbish trucks cleared up debris on some of the larger streets.
Widespread looting took place across the cities of Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas.
Macron said local prefects and mayors would draft measures to protect shops and civic buildings.
The president also said there would be "full transparency" over the police response to the demonstrations.
Tear gas and water cannon were turned on crowds over the weekend and riot police were seen hitting people with batons in several places.
France's interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously.
Student protests that began last month escalated significantly on Saturday after they were joined by trade union members and other anti-government groups.
The response from political figures has pointed to France's deep political divisions as the country prepares for an election in April which could see the hard-right pitted against the hard-left.
France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that while demonstrating was a fundamental right, there were "outrages" committed by "several thousand far-left individuals" who were determined to target public buildings and confront the police.
Later, they were joined by "delinquents who looted and ransacked numerous businesses in several cities in France", he said.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon - leader of the hard-left La France Insoumise party - heavily criticised Nuñez and police chiefs on social media.
He said they had "shown complete incompetence" with their handling of the demonstrations and called them "specialists in organised chaos".
Meanwhile, the leader of the hard-right National Rally party, Marine Le Pen, condemned the "exploitation" of anger "by political forces that encourage violence".

articles.title_orig: This Pocket-Sized Multitool Is An Affordable Leatherman Alternative
articles.title_zh: This Pocket-Sized Multitool Is An Affordable Leatherman Alternative
articles.content_orig:
Not every job calls for an entire crew armed to the teeth with a bunch of tools. Sometimes, for stuff like a loose bolt, a one-size-fits-all solution works best – like a pocket multitool . Here, people typically go for Leatherman, a company that claims to have built the first pliers-based multitool. Among its offerings, the Leatherman Wave+, a full-size multi-tool, is one of the most popular options in its category.
Plenty of Leatherman rivals try to undercut these offerings on price, but one of the more interesting upcoming options comes from Tsuchioto Works, a Tokyo design studio. It's called the Blackjaw, a pocket-sized gadget that folds pliers, two blades, a saw, two screwdrivers, two openers, and a carabiner into a single frame. Folded up, it measures just 4.2 inches long and weighs 7.8 ounces. That may be slightly longer than the Wave+, which measures 4 inches, but it's also noticeably lighter at 7.8 ounces versus the 8.5 ounces of the Wave+. It clips to your belt loop with the built-in carabiner, so it's always within reach.
However, the real sell here is the price. The Blackjaw is being sold through a Kickstarter crowdfunding campaign right now, and the campaign price sits at $90. That's significantly lower than the $129.95 tag on the Wave+. Shipping to the U.S. adds another $15, but even with it, you're still only at $105. You can also further knock off a few bucks with the Super Early Bird tier, taking the price down to around $80. That said, Tsuchioto plans to charge $119 once the campaign ends. Unfortunately, backers will have to wait a while to actually get the product since Tsuchioto doesn't expect to start shipping the Blackjaw until March 2027.
Price aside, the biggest difference between the Blackjaw and the Wave+ is that none of the parts on the Blackjaw are detachable. Having no detachable parts means you won't accidentally lose a set of bits, meaning to can complete a job. The downside, however, is that the tool is left with just two drivers, a Phillips and a flathead.
As for the Blackjaw itself, the name pretty much spells out the design. The tool is essentially a pair of plier jaws with two handles, with almost the whole thing wearing a matte black finish. While the handles are aluminum, the blades, jaws, and drivers are made of stainless steel. Since every implement here folds out from the outer side of the two handles, you can use the blade or driver without first having to unfold the pliers.
All in all, you get 11 tools on the Blackjaw, including that carabiner. There's the plier head designed to stack long-nose tips for small parts, a toothed jaw for nuts and pipe, and a wire cutter. Then there's the double-sided saw for handling small branches and dowels. The can and bottle openers cover meals at the camp. A separate notch is designed for stripping wire. Finally, the knife is designed for boxes and cord. So overall, it's a complete tool that can handle a lot of jobs, and undercuts its chief competitor in price by a fair bit.

articles.title_orig: Gold edges higher as softer oil eases inflation woes
articles.title_zh: Gold edges higher as softer oil eases inflation woes
articles.content_orig:
Kitco NEWS has a diverse team of journalists reporting on the economy, stock markets, commodities, cryptocurrencies, mining and metals with accuracy and objectivity. Our goal is to help people make informed market decisions through in-depth reporting, daily market roundups, interviews with prominent industry figures, comprehensive coverage (often exclusive) of important industry events and analyses of market-affecting developments.
(Kitco News) – Gold prices staged a late-week recovery after coming under heavy pressure from hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data, rising Treasury yields, and a firmer dollar, as falling bond yields and reduced expectations for an October Federal Reserve rate hike helped the precious metal recover much of its losses.
Spot gold kicked off the week trading at $4,193.59 per ounce on Sunday evening, and the yellow metal briefly climbed above $4,200 as traders continued to monitor the U.S.-Iran conflict and inflation risks from elevated energy prices. The advance quickly faded, however, with gold setting its weekly high at $4,216.91 per ounce on Monday before a stronger dollar and rising Treasury yields pushed prices lower through Tuesday’s trading session.
The selling accelerated Wednesday after September CPI rose 3.7% annually, exceeding expectations and reinforcing concerns that energy-driven inflation could force the Fed to tighten monetary policy again. Gold broke below $4,100 and set its weekly low at $4,073.35 per ounce at noon on Wednesday, as traders increased bets on an October rate hike and the dollar strengthened.
Gold rebounded Thursday despite another hotter-than-expected inflation reading from the Producer Price Index, as Treasury yields retreated sharply from recent highs while the dollar weakened. The recovery carried into Friday after Fed Chair Kevin Warsh on Thursday evening refrained from signaling an October rate increase, helping reduce immediate tightening expectations even as markets continued to anticipate another hike before year-end. Gold briefly approached $4,200 once again before stopping short and surrendering some of its gains to trade marginally lower on the week and the session heading into the weekend.
The latest Kitco News Weekly Gold Survey showed half of Wall Street on the fence on gold’s near-term price direction, while less than half of Main Street sentiment creeped closer to a bearish majority after another failed breakout.
“I am neutral on gold for the coming week,” said Colin Cieszynski, chief market strategist at SIA Wealth Management. “Gold appears to be hanging around the $4,200 level at the moment and there is less economic data due next week to move it as focus turns to corporate earnings.”
“Up,” said Darin Newsom, senior market analyst at Barchart.com. “I don’t care about technical (Dec gold is in an intermediate-term uptrend on its weekly chart) or fundamental (central banks around the world continue to buy gold) analysis at this point. What got my attention was the US president reportedly saying he ‘won’t use nuclear weapons or send ground troops to Iran.’ Which means he is likely planning on doing just that. Given this, long-term investors might get interested in gold again if everything else is destroyed over the weekend. I’ll spend this weekend watching the 1964 classic ‘Dr. Strangelove’ and listening to R.E.M.’s ‘It’s the End of the World as We Know It.’”
“Unchanged,” said Adrian Day, president of Adrian Day Asset Management. “I remain in the camp that sees some more back and forth before gold breaks out.  It is coming soon, however.  Gold’s resilience in the face of a run-up in yields, and relatively strong dollar and oil prices, is telling.  Gold is well supported on the downside, so it’s now a matter of time before it breaks out. But an end to the war – which would bring with it a lower dollar and lower oil price leading to reduced inflation and rate hike expectations – is the likely catalyst.”
“Up,” said James Stanley, senior market strategist at Forex.com. “Strong late-week response, and while there’s still a case for continued digestion as price is building in a falling wedge pattern, I still want to bias this as ‘up’ until I have reason not to. The $4k level in spot remains the major level of note, and until there’s a convincing breach of that, I’m probably going to remain bullish.”
Fawad Razaqzada, market analyst at StoneX Bullion, said that despite gold’s midweek rebound, he remains doubtful prices have seen a bottom.
“Yes, the US dollar has eased a bit and the reversal in Treasury yields are also helping,” he said. “But while the immediate pressure has eased, I would be reluctant to interpret [Thursday’s] gains as a clear signal that the correction is over. For now, at least, my near-term gold outlook remains modestly bearish, even if I have a strong long-term bullish bias towards gold and especially silver.”
Razaqzada said he is waiting for confirmation that gold has formed a low. “The metal has tried to hold key support around $4,100, but the resistance zone overhead has held firm,” he said. “I would need to see a move above that zone before turning bullish at current levels. Thus, the technical gold outlook still hangs in the balance.”
“Up,” said Rich Checkan, president and COO of Asset Strategies International. “With the U.S. dollar weakening for the first time in five weeks, gold should benefit. Buyers of gold in currencies other than the U.S. dollar will find their gold ultimately cheaper with the more favorable exchange rate.”
Naeem Aslam, chief investment officer at Zaye Capital Markets, believes gold’s outlook will depend on whether persistent inflation outweighs the pressure from potentially elevated interest rates.
“Thursday’s retreat in Treasury yields and the dollar provided support for bullion despite stronger wholesale inflation, demonstrating that gold responds to changing real-yield expectations rather than inflation figures alone,” he said. “Analysts should monitor the $4,154 price area as near-term support and $4,179 as immediate resistance, alongside Treasury yields, dollar strength, central bank guidance and developments affecting global energy supplies. A sustained decline in real yields could encourage additional institutional diversification into gold, while renewed monetary tightening expectations may trigger consolidation. We therefore see inflation uncertainty, geopolitical hedging and shifting monetary policy expectations as the principal forces shaping gold’s price direction through the remainder of 2026.”
“Lower,” said Adam Button, head of currency strategy at investingLive. “I struggle to see how the Fed only hikes by the 70 bps that's now priced into the curve. This week's inflation data was a big problem that's being overlooked because of the worries about AI debt.”
Daniel Pavilonis, senior commodities broker at StoneX Group, told Kitco News that gold remains an inverse 10-year Treasury yield play, with the rise and fall of the yield determining whether investors should be long or short the precious metal.
“We're seeing something similar to what we saw in the seventies, with high interest rates and sticky inflation,” he said. “Certain sectors of the markets or the economy do well... and other ones don't. Right now, it seems like AI is pretty strong with the infrastructure buildouts. But maybe there's some truth to [the idea] that it's not just the energy sector that's driving inflation, but also this demand structure from the AI boom, and instead of money going into buying U.S. Treasuries or something like that, they're spending the money on AI infrastructure.”

articles.title_orig: Indonesian stocks plunge to six-year low as MSCI downgrade fears mount
articles.title_zh: Indonesian stocks plunge to six-year low as MSCI downgrade fears mount
articles.content_orig:
Indonesia's benchmark stock index plunged over 5% on Monday to its lowest level in six years, as concerns over a potential downgrade by MSCI intensified fears of further foreign investor outflows.
The Jakarta Composite Index tumbled to its lowest level since early October 2020, extending a bruising sell-off in Indonesian equities. MSCI, the index provider, on Friday proposed reclassifying Indonesia directly from an emerging market to stand-alone status, raising the prospect of the country's removal from major global equity benchmarks.
MSCI is expected to make a final decision by June, with the potential reclassification hinging on whether Indonesian authorities can demonstrate meaningful improvements in market governance and transparency.
Goldman Sachs warned in a Sunday note that a full removal from MSCI's emerging-market indexes could trigger approximately $5.6 billion in passive fund outflows, equivalent to 18 days of average daily trading volume for constituents of the MSCI Indonesia Investable Market Index.
An additional $2.7 billion could be at risk if FTSE Russell subsequently takes similar action, although the bank stressed that such a move would be a separate scenario.
Goldman estimated that active funds benchmarked to MSCI and FTSE indexes hold more than $8 billion in Indonesian equities, although any selling by these investors would be discretionary rather than automatically triggered by a downgrade.
The bank maintained its underweight rating on Indonesian equities, citing persistent index uncertainty, weak corporate earnings and macroeconomic headwinds.
"Valuations have compressed significantly, but remain above historical troughs; index, earnings, and macro risks constrain a re-rating," Goldman strategists led by Alvin So wrote.
The MSCI Indonesia Index has fallen 47% this year as of Friday, data provided by the bank showed, with foreign investors withdrawing a net $5.1 billion from Indonesian equities over the period.
Foreign ownership of Indonesian stocks has declined to 25% in October from 27% in January, while the value of foreign holdings has nearly halved to approximately $130 billion from $250 billion, the bank said.
Despite the steep declines, Goldman cautioned that Indonesian equities may not have bottomed. The MSCI Indonesia Index's 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratio has fallen to 7.3 times, its lowest level since the global financial crisis, but remains above historical troughs.
The strategists also expect Indonesia's central bank to raise interest rates twice more, by 25 basis points each in the fourth quarter of 2026 and first quarter of 2027, potentially adding further pressure to economic growth and equity valuations.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Officials Condemn West Bank Attacks as Netanyahu Casts Doubt on Them
articles.title_zh: U.S. Officials Condemn West Bank Attacks as Netanyahu Casts Doubt on Them
articles.content_orig:
Israeli police said on Monday they had arrested 10 suspects as part of an investigation into violent incidents in the occupied-West Bank over the weekend, including separate attacks on a Washington Post photojournalist and European diplomats.
The United States, Israel’s closest ally, had urged a crackdown on settler violence and the arrest of the perpetrators of the attack on the Washington Post photojournalist. France, Belgium and Poland, whose diplomats were attacked, also called on Israel to take action.
Police said the suspects were arrested in a pre-dawn operation on suspicion of involvement in acts of violence, violating a closed military zone order and illegal construction.
The suspects, whom police did not identify, were taken into custody for questioning. Israel’s Army Radio reported that they were Israeli citizens.
Prosecutions of Israeli settlers are rare.
A video released by the police of the pre-dawn operation appeared to show at least one arrested suspect, whose face is not seen, wearing ritual tassels known as tzitzit, which are often worn by observant Jewish men.
The video also appeared to show two slingshots, which can be used to hurl stones, being found at one property. On Friday, when the Washington Post journalist was attacked, dozens of masked settlers, some armed, descended on a Palestinian olive harvest, with some settlers hurling stones with slingshots.
Police, military forces and the Shin Bet domestic security service took part in the operation.
Referring to the West Bank by its biblical name, Judea and Samaria, Israeli police commissioner Daniel Levy said the law applied to everyone, “regardless of identity or affiliation.”
“The Israel Police is committed to professional, equal, and impartial law enforcement, based on evidence and in accordance with the law,” he said in a statement announcing the arrests.
Masked Israeli settlers were filmed on Friday assaulting Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, a U.S. citizen, who was covering a Palestinian olive harvest in the West Bank. Levine was taken to hospital and underwent surgery on a finger.
On Saturday, French, Belgian and Polish diplomats as well as a French mayor were attacked by masked settlers in another part of the West Bank. A Belgian diplomatic vehicle was also damaged.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and the military have blamed “Israeli rioters” for the attack on the diplomats.
However, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose religious-nationalist coalition is projected to lose its governing majority at the October 27 election, has been more circumspect.
He has said the diplomats entered a “sensitive area with a history of confrontations” and without coordinating with the military. He has also said that the facts ​of the attack on Levine were “unclear.”
Levine has said she was attacked by masked men wearing tzitzit tassels. Israel’s President Isaac Herzog has apologised, saying the “violent rioters” who “brutally attacked” her did not represent the values of Israel.
Settler attacks ​on the Palestinians ⁠are surging, with at least 170 since September 27, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group. Journalists, Israeli activists and foreign observers have also been targeted.

articles.title_orig: North Carolina has the lowest gas prices in the country. Some say it's still too high
articles.title_zh: North Carolina has the lowest gas prices in the country. Some say it's still too high
articles.content_orig:
More than a week after North Carolina lawmakers voted to suspend the gas tax, the state now has the lowest gas prices on average in the entire country.
Several people WRAL spoke with on Sunday still aren't satisfied.
“They're still high. Still a lot of money out of my paycheck," gas station customer Hayden Epperson said.
As of Sunday, a gallon of unleaded gas in Raleigh costs an average of $3.62, nearly 35 cents cheaper than a week ago. A gallon of diesel in Raleigh costs $5.62, about 28 cents cheaper than a week ago.
However, it wasn't lost on Epperson just how much lower prices were one year ago. On Oct. 18, 2025, gas cost $2.78 and diesel cost $3.52.
"It's ridiculous. It takes half a tank to get to work. A half tank to get back. And it's not good," Epperson said.
The high costs aren't just affecting commuters driving more than 30 minutes to get to work. Lisa Penny, a farmer's wife who grows produce in Benson, said the high diesel prices are capping off a difficult year for farming.
"Having to buy diesel in bulk has been very, very strenuous and made it hard for us as farmers to keep all the pricing for all of our produce at a low cost," Penny said.
While the gas tax suspension was signed into law on Friday, Oct. 9, it didn't start until days later . Many faced the same prices for days after it was signed. Petroleum analyst Patrick De Haan said there could be a few reasons why.
"It's hard to lower the prices immediately when stations already paid a much higher price for the fuel that's in their tanks," De Haan said. "It takes a few days for them for stations to sell through their existing taxed inventory before they're able to buy the non-taxed fuel. That's why it's taken about a week to to kind of fully realize the the tax suspension."
De Haan said a common misunderstanding about the gas tax he noticed is that gas should be exactly 41 cents lower since the tax suspension was signed into law, but he warned the tax suspension is only one small factor in the price people pay for fuel.
"The tax is suspended, but that doesn't freeze the price of oil from suddenly going up," De Haan said. "The price of oil is moving every day and in the last week it's actually gone up fairly noticeably. This is one of the rare times in my career where beyond a few days out, it's impossible to predict because it's it's not about normal market ebbs and flows right now.
De Haan added that the ongoing war with Iran makes prices extremely volatile, and it's possible they may shoot up again even with the tax out of the picture.
"It's about geopolitical tensions and developments that can happen at a moment's notice," De Haan added. "It depends on what's going on between the US and Iran and Ukraine and Russia."
The gas tax is set to go back in effect December 1.

International Maritime Organization Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez discusses efforts to communicate with Tehran as attacks escalate and commercial shipping faces growing risks.
Thousands of sailors remain stranded near the Strait of Hormuz amid escalating attacks on commercial ships, the United Nations' top maritime official warned Sunday after Iran accused the U.S. military of using an international emergency radio channel to threaten civilian crews.
The warning also came amid reports that 24 ships had been attacked on the waterway over roughly two weeks, underscoring growing concerns about maritime safety in the region, according to Financial Times .
"The situation continues to be severe and critical when it comes to international shipping," International Maritime Organization (IMO) Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez told Fox News Digital.
"There is a double blockade and too many vessels have been attacked, particularly in recent days.
'VAST MAJORITY' OF IRAN'S ATTEMPTED ATTACKS ON STRAIT OF HORMUZ ARE UNSUCCESSFUL, CENTCOM SPOKESMAN SAYS
24 ships have been attacked on the waterway over roughly two weeks, according to reports. (Fatemeh Bahrami / Anadolu via Getty Images)
"Seafarers have continued to perish in these attacks and around 6,000 seafarers remain trapped since the beginning of the conflict," he warned, adding that his message was not to transit the Strait of Hormuz or put seafarers at risk "until we have guarantees."
Dominguez's warning followed an Oct. 9 letter to the IMO in which Iran alleged that the U.S. military used VHF Channel 16 , an internationally designated maritime distress and safety channel, to intimidate Iranian crews in the Persian Gulf.
"VHF Channel 16 has been repeatedly occupied for prolonged periods by the United States military forces operating in the Persian Gulf," the letter stated.
TRUMP OPENS HORMUZ UNDER FIRE WITH ‘PROJECT FREEDOM’ AS IRAN WARNS OF ATTACKS
Smoke column rises from tanker El Gaia after incident in the Strait of Hormuz.
"During such transmissions, Iranian seafarers have been addressed in Persian with threatening, abusive and provocative language and in certain instances urged to abandon their vessels."
In a statement to Fox News Digital, U.S. Central Command defended its enforcement of the naval blockade of Iranian ports .
"The U.S. naval blockade has been in place for months and is professionally communicated to all international mariners," CENTCOM said.
"Vessels that refuse to comply with blockade enforcement receive multiple warnings, with ample opportunity to comply.
"American forces remain highly vigilant, focused, and professional while fully enforcing the naval blockade against Iran ."
Iran's complaint was submitted by Seyed Ali Mousavi, its ambassador to the IMO, and circulated to member states on Oct. 9, according to a copy reviewed by Fox News Digital.
Tehran also accused American forces of turning the maritime safety channel into an "instrument of military intimidation and psychological pressure against civilian crews."
The letter cited commercial vessels, shipping companies and maritime operators but provided no recordings, transcripts or specific details of the alleged exchanges. Fox News Digital could not independently verify the accusations.
IRAN THREATENS TO HALT RED SEA TRAFFIC IN RESPONSE TO US MILITARY BLOCKADE OF PORTS
Naval units from Iran simulate the rescue of a hijacked vessel during joint drills at the Port of Bandar Abbas in Hormozgan, Iran, on Feb. 19, 2026. (Iranian Army/Handout/Anadolu via Getty Images)
"Seafarers are not trained for combat, and they are not guilty of any conflicts that are happening around the world," Dominguez said.
"And we have seen this in several parts of the world where Channel 16, that should not be used for this kind of communication, starts receiving messages that may be perceived as actually threatening or that are outside the remit of why it was created."
Iran also asked the IMO to raise its allegations with member states and relevant international organizations, potentially including the International Telecommunication Union.
Dominguez said the IMO could review its regulations and procedures to determine whether stronger safeguards are needed, though he did not announce a formal investigation.
"Our role here at IMO is that when those situations take place, we will then look into any technical measures or any operational aspects that we may need to clarify further within our regulatory framework," he said, stressing that member states have equal rights to raise concerns, regardless of the conflict.
"We have a responsibility, and I have a duty as well, to circulate letters and notes that the countries actually put forward when they're also being affected."
WHO CONTROLS THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ RIGHT NOW? HERE'S WHAT THE SHIP TRAFFIC ACTUALLY SHOWS
The U.S. naval blockade has been in place for months and is professionally communicated to all international mariners, CENTCOM said. (U.S. Navy)
"We take all that information, meet at the level of different meetings of the organization and have the discussions," Dominguez added.
"If it's demonstrated that we probably need to improve our rules in order to avoid communications issues, or that we need to enhance the knowledge of how these channels should be used, that is a role for us."
The IMO had recorded 100 confirmed maritime incidents across the region as of Oct. 9, with 24 seafarers killed since the conflict began Feb. 28. Dominguez also warned that fraudulent ship registrations and false flags have become major contributors to the danger.
"What we've also seen right now is an increase in fraudulent registries with false flags that are taking the risk and acting as shuttle tankers in order to bring goods in and out," he said. "That's one of the reasons that we're seeing an escalation.
"And it's the irresponsible shipowners that are taking the risk in order to actually be able to trade and move some of the goods and the cargoes."
WHITE HOUSE SILENT ON IRAN-OMAN HORMUZ PLAN TEHRAN SAYS WOULD BAN US WARSHIPS
A ship is seen passing through the Strait of Hormuz during a two-week temporary ceasefire between the United States and Iran on April 8, 2026. (Shady Alassar/Anadolu/Getty Images)
"For me, any single case, any vessel that is attacked, any life of a seafarer that is lost, is a critical situation for me, because they are all relevant, they are all important."
Despite the confrontation, Dominguez said diplomatic channels with Iran remain open, though he has no direct contact with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
"I have communications with all the member states of IMO, and that includes the Islamic Republic of Iran," he said.
"Of course, that's through the diplomatic channels. I don't have direct contact with the IRGC .
"I have conversations with them and they respond to my messages. You know, the information flows. What is difficult is to get final decisions because of the conflict that is ongoing."

articles.title_orig: California woman indicted on charges that she was spying for China
articles.title_zh: California woman indicted on charges that she was spying for China
articles.content_orig:
A California woman who prosecutors allege was spying on a son of Taiwan’s president was indicted this month on charges of conspiracy and being an unregistered foreign agent for China.
The indictment was filed Oct. 9 in U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, and the allegations it lays out mirror an earlier criminal complaint against the woman, Wanying Zhang, 34, of Irvine.
Prosecutors say Zhang, who also goes by Heather, spied on a son of Taiwan’s president outside his home in the Seattle area at the behest of Chinese officials. The spying is alleged to have taken place between roughly June and September 2025, prosecutors claim.
Taiwan is a self-ruled democracy that is the source of 90% of the world’s “leading-edge chip manufacturing,” according to the U.S. International Trade Administration . China claims Taiwan, which the U.S. has recognized for nearly half a century, though it is required by law to ensure Taiwan can defend itself.
Prosecutors allege Zhang was under the direction of an unnamed Chinese government official and former classmate at her alma mater, China’s University of International Relations, which is “closely affiliated with China’s intelligence apparatus,” an FBI investigator said in earlier court documents.
An example of the alleged activity was a request by the former classmate to send him pictures “of the house” where the son lives, according to the indictment.
Prosecutors alleged that Zhang flew from California to Las Vegas and then to the Seattle area to conduct surveillance of the unidentified son and his home from outside.
The indictment alleges she captured photos, video and license plate information and sent them to the person alleged to be her Chinese handler. An unidentified person, who had fled to China in September, was with her, prosecutors said.
Zhang also traveled to China in August 2025 to meet with a Chinese government official, returned days later and told the official she would most likely be going to where the victim was the following week, according to the indictment.
Her lawyer, Craig Harbaugh, did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday.
Previously, Harbaugh, a veteran criminal defense attorney, described Zhang as an upstanding resident of Irvine, about 42 miles southeast of Los Angeles, where she lives with her husband and two young daughters.
“The government’s theory — she’s been a sleeper agent for the last 10 years, working as a real estate agent, raising her family and will choose to go to China and abandon her work, her family and her home — it’s not supported,” Harbaugh said in court Oct. 7.
U.S. Magistrate Judge Steve Kim ordered Zhang held in pretrial detention after prosecutors argued she poses a flight risk. The U.S. Bureau of Prisons website shows that she remains in custody.
Zhang is scheduled to appear in federal district court Friday for a post-indictment arraignment. She could face up to 15 years in prison.
David Douglas is a supervising producer for NBC News based in Los Angeles.

articles.title_orig: Grass fire at Canadian military base kills 4 soldiers and critically injures 19 other people
articles.title_zh: Grass fire at Canadian military base kills 4 soldiers and critically injures 19 other people
articles.content_orig:
Four members of the Canadian military have died and dozens were injured at a base in the province of Alberta after a fire broke out in a grassy training area and spread rapidly due to strong winds.
Addressing the nation on Sunday from Ottawa, Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime".
The fire broke out at about 16:00 local time (22:00 GMT) on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of the country's busiest military training bases, and is now contained.
"The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces who we have lost," said Carney.
The BBC has confirmed that Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding and Pte Hayden Lykkemark have died.
Of the 39 injured people being cared for in hospital, at least 19 are in a critical condition, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said at a press briefing on Sunday evening.
Fire and rescue teams are remaining at the scene to contain any potential flare-ups, Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh told the BBC.
Members of the infantry had been conducting "high-intensity combat training with live munitions" at a grenade range and attack range, where 10 soldiers practise attacking a simulated enemy, Maj-Gen Wade Rutland told reporters at the briefing.
"There was a multitude of ordnance moving through the Wainwright training area," he said, including a grenade launcher, grenades, small arms and ammunition.
A grass fire ignited about 1km (0.6 miles) away, with the cause currently under investigation, and moved toward the attack range.
"What I would say is there was multiple training activities happening throughout the training area at the time," he  said. "Uncommonly strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction towards the range administrative area."
Cannon fire had been heard coming from the base on Saturday before it suddenly stopped, Mayor Pugh told the BBC, noting it's not uncommon to hear cannons being fired there.
News then came through that local emergency services had been deployed to an "all hands on deck" situation.
Carney said military and emergency crews fought the flames throughout the night in "some of the worst conditions imaginable".
The people who were hurt were on the attack range and included reservists and soldiers from the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, officials said.
In a statement early on Sunday, the Canadian Armed Forces said that "while the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity".
Rutland told the briefing: "We do not believe this [incident] to be a result of any oil and gas infrastructure nor any outside interference".
Wainwright, about 210km (130 miles) east of Edmonton, Alberta's capital, is one of the main bases used by the Canadian military for live-fire training exercises, and it houses troops from Canada and allied countries. About 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers are on site on a typical day.
Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told broadcaster CBC that the number of patients involved in the incident had "completely overwhelmed" healthcare facilities in Wainwright.
The Royal Alexandra Hospital is in Edmonton, where patients are being transferred. The hospital at first declared a code orange - a disaster-response protocol for a high-casualty incident. That has since been stood down.
The provincial health agency said in a statement on Sunday that it deployed 30 units directly into Wainwright, including 22 ground ambulances, six fixed-wing and two rotary wing units.
"It is anticipated that care for patients impacted by this incident will be intensive and will add to existing high demand on acute care in Alberta," it said, adding that patients were being treated at facilities across the province.
STARS, the regional air ambulance service, said aircraft and crews from Edmonton, Saskatoon, and Calgary had been deployed.
Brandon Simmons, who lives in long-term care at the Wainwright Health Centre, told Reuters that when code orange was announced, nurses dropped everything and immediately started grabbing stretchers, gurneys and medical equipment before running to the front entrance.
Ambulances kept coming "throughout the night", he said.
"I heard people screaming inside of those vehicles that will never end up being out of my mind," he recalled, saying it was "like a scene from a war movie".
Additional reporting by Lisa Lambert

articles.title_orig: Albania's Prime Minister Edi Rama ignores calls to resign amid violent clashes
articles.title_zh: Albania's Prime Minister Edi Rama ignores calls to resign amid violent clashes
articles.content_orig:
Student-led protests continued in Albania for a sixth day with continued demands for Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
Despite those calls, Rama is refusing to step down , saying the demonstrations were not a threat to government but rather a threat to Albania's ambition of accession to the European Union.
"I ​am not being challenged, the government is not being challenged, a government majority or a winning party in the elections is not being challenged but a path is being challenged, a mission is being challenged," Rama said in a live address on Facebook.
"Albanians need to think ​very clearly: Do they want this, do they want that, or do they want the EU?” Rama asked.
Rama ruled out resigning and said that the protests were the "work of an outside hand," without further clarification.
Earlier in the week Rama ruled out resigning, saying that governments were changed through elections.
Student-led demonstrations, spurred by discontent over alleged government corruption, unemployment and poor education standards, have rocked central Tirana and spread to other cities in the past week.
On Sunday, hundreds gathered outside the Education Ministry , chanting "Rama resign!" and threw rocks ​at riot police who responded with tear gas, water cannon and rubber bullets.
The protests come at a difficult for Albania as it is among a group of Balkan states seeking to join the EU by 2030.
There have been calls for calm from Brussels amid the violent protests. The European Commission in Sunday condemned the use of ⁠violence ⁠in Tirana and othern cities.
The commission added that it welcomed the Albanian authorities' ​commitment that the right to protest will ​be protected.

articles.title_orig: Burnham warns of Neets-fuelled 'economic catastrophe and moral failure'
articles.title_zh: Burnham warns of Neets-fuelled 'economic catastrophe and moral failure'
articles.content_orig:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned the UK faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" due to the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training.
Writing in the Times newspaper , Burnham has laid out his case for the government to "invest in the success of our young people" rather than "pay for failure through the benefits system".
"Benefits will become the backstop, not the starting point," Burnham wrote in his piece published in Monday's paper.
Later this week, the government is expected to announce plans to give young people thousands of job opportunities. The Conservative Party has labelled the government's youth employment strategy "a disaster".
According to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics, there are almost a million people aged 16 to 24 known as Neets - not in education, employment or training.
In his opinion column, the prime minister said this reflected a "generation being denied its chance to get on in life".
"This is an economic catastrophe and a moral failure. And it must change," he wrote.
Burnham said two years of Covid lockdowns, social media that erodes "confidence and sense of belonging", an education system focused on the "university route", job markets with "too few opportunities" and failures of previous governments have all contributed to the Neets crisis.
"Today, the welfare system provides an assessment, a payment and, after that, goodbye," Burnham wrote. "Too often there is no support, no offer of skills and no opportunity to get a job."
He flagged a shift in the approach to welfare, which he said "will no longer begin by establishing which benefits a young person is entitled to" but rather "begin with their ambitions and the help they need to achieve them".
The prime minister added: "The safety net will always be there for those who cannot work. But if someone can work with the right help, the government has a duty to do everything in its power to make that happen."
Ministers are this week set to release plans for tens of thousands of new youth apprenticeships and placements in the construction industry, and at accounting, consulting and legal firms.
Shadow Business and Trade Secretary Julia Lopez said: "Labour have been a disaster for youth jobs. Their tax hikes and red tape have made it harder for businesses to hire, invest and grow, destroying opportunities for young people looking to take their first step on the career ladder."
Burnham confirmed the long-awaited full review of young people and work will be published next month, and vowed to take its recommendations "seriously".
The review's author, former health secretary Alan Milburn, has argued for the need to "redistribute money from the welfare system to more employment support" in an interview with the Guardian published on Sunday.
"This is not a workshy, snowflake generation," Milburn said. "If we provide more opportunities and we provide more support, the overwhelming majority of young people will take that, because that's what they want. The system isn't delivering what young people want, which is a job."
Milburn calculated that the government spends 25 times more on benefits for young people than getting them into work, describing the current rate of Neets as "shameful" .
Chancellor John Healey, who is due to hand down his first budget on 28 October, told the Labour party conference in September the government had a "moral duty" to address welfare spending.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic commits 5% of shares to ‘public benefit’ fund
articles.title_zh: Anthropic commits 5% of shares to ‘public benefit’ fund
articles.content_orig:
Today, we’re committing a portion of Anthropic’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows. Subject to stockholder approval, 5% of Anthropic’s shares will be committed today, with an additional 2% added at the board’s discretion for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a set baseline.
As a public benefit corporation, most of our work in pursuit of our mission takes place inside the company: research relevant to AI safety and interpretability; applied biomedical research; discounts on Claude for nonprofits and scientific institutions. These activities have both a public benefit component and for-profit value, so we house them directly in the company.
The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will have increased flexibility and scale, enabling us to pursue our mission in new ways: for example, we might explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.
One example is labor market impacts. AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers. Anthropic has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.
We’re establishing the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund as a wholly-owned LLC—rather than a 501(c)(3) or other format—to give adjustability between different forms of giving. None of the Anthropic equity held by the LLC will be used for lobbying or political giving, in the US or abroad.
Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good. It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit.
This builds on commitments our co-founders and employees have already made. When Anthropic was founded, our co-founders pledged to donate 80% of their equity holdings, and since founding we have also operated an equity donation match program that allows employees to pledge equity which Anthropic matches. Approximately half of our employees participate in this program. When combined with today’s announcement, roughly 20% of Anthropic shares will be dedicated to the public good, plus any additional percentage that could be added if the company reaches specific valuation milestones.
In the coming months, we will share more about the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund’s structure and governance, including the valuation milestones that may add to its stake. We will also report on our progress to date against our mission in an upcoming public benefit report.
To evaluate the safety of our systems, Anthropic is giving employee-like access to a team from METR, a nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models, and we're in early discussions with several other organizations, including Hugging Face.
Earlier this year, we shared an update on our election safeguards. Here, we outline how we’ve continued to strengthen these safeguards ahead of this year’s US midterms.

articles.content_orig:
Nvidia ( NVDA -1.43% ) has made investors significantly richer over the past four years, turning a $10,000 investment into nearly $179,000 as of this writing.
This massive surge in Nvidia's shares has been fueled by the advent of artificial intelligence (AI). When OpenAI's ChatGPT , introduced publicly in November 2022, became a big hit, companies lined up to buy Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs) after it emerged that the semiconductor giant's chips played an instrumental role in training the chatbot.
The AI economy and Nvidia have come a long way since then. AI is now finding its way into several industries, boosting productivity and economic growth. The good news for Nvidia investors is that AI adoption isn't showing any signs of slowing, which explains why the company continues to deliver robust growth even after becoming significantly larger over the past four years.
We will take a closer look at the company's prospects in this article and assess whether investing $10,000 in Nvidia stock over the next five years could be a profitable move.
Nvidia's AI-driven surge has made it the world's largest company with a market cap of $5.2 trillion. So, expecting another 20x jump in Nvidia's stock price over the next five years would be quite absurd, as it would put its market cap past $100 trillion. However, that doesn't mean Nvidia stock can't climb higher over the next five years.
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 10/16/26
After all, the company is still growing at an impressive pace despite the scale it has achieved. Nvidia's revenue in the first six months of fiscal 2027 (which will end in January 2027) increased by 96% over the same period last year to $177.8 billion. The company expects fiscal Q3 revenue of $108 billion, an 89% jump from the year-ago period.
Analysts expect a 91% spike in Nvidia's revenue for fiscal 2027 to $411.6 billion. Meanwhile, earnings per share are expected to almost double in fiscal 2027 to $9.31. Importantly, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is confident that the company's growth will continue unabated next year. He recently noted at a conference that the number of chips the company sells will double in 2027, according to CNBC .
Huang added that continued investments in AI infrastructure will drive this incredible growth, as companies and governments look to make the most of the technology's benefits. For example, the World Economic Forum noted earlier this year that AI could increase labor productivity by 1.5% to 3% over the next decade, citing the chief economist of consulting giant EY.
Moreover, investors will do well to note that AI is moving beyond data centers into real-world applications, such as robots and cars. Known as physical AI, Nvidia is pushing into this niche where machines can make complex decisions on their own. From performing precision-related tasks such as threading needles in surgical wards to operating on a conveyor belt, Nvidia is moving into a new frontier that could supercharge its long-term growth.
Nvidia's physical AI offerings are already being used by the likes of Amazon and Japan's national AI venture, and I won't be surprised to see the tech giant pulling in more customers. That's because the physical AI market's revenue is expected to grow to 430 billion euros by 2030, suggesting this niche could move the needle significantly for Nvidia over the next five years.
Throw in the $3 trillion to $4 trillion revenue opportunity that Nvidia sees in the AI infrastructure market in 2030, and it is easy to see why analysts have become extremely bullish about its growth prospects through fiscal 2029 (which will end in January 2029).
NVDA Revenue Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts
According to the above chart, Nvidia's revenue could increase by 68% in fiscal 2028, which is almost in line with the company's guidance of 70% growth. That's expected to be followed by a 30% increase in fiscal 2029 to $900 billion. There is a solid chance Nvidia will maintain strong growth in fiscal years 2030 and 2031 as well, which could set the stock up for further gains.
Let's assume Nvidia's top line increases by even 10% in fiscal 2030 and 2031 (which will end in January 2031), its top line could reach $1.09 trillion in 2030 (given that fiscal 2031 will coincide with the majority of calendar 2030).
Now, this AI stock trades at 18 times sales. Assuming Nvidia trades at half of this sales multiple after five years, its market cap could jump to $9.8 trillion (based on the $1.09 trillion revenue estimate). That implies a potential upside of 88% from current levels. So, a $10,000 investment in this semiconductor stock will be worth more than $18,800 by 2030.
However, that could be a conservative estimate, as Nvidia could grow faster and command a premium valuation after five years. That's why investors can still consider buying this AI bellwether, as it has the potential to make investors richer owing to emerging niches within the AI ecosystem.

articles.title_orig: 3 Essential Tools Every PC Gamer Should Install
articles.title_zh: 3 Essential Tools Every PC Gamer Should Install
articles.content_orig:
Just because you've built or bought a gaming PC doesn't mean you fully understand the hardware inside, though there are essential tips every beginner should know . You'll want to wrap your head around this knowledge to get the best performance out of your games, whether they're AAA or indie. That means you need the right tools for the job, and with so many to choose from, it's easy to get lost in the weeds with apps that often overcomplicate things or overlap with the OS's built-in tools. With proper guidance, it's easy enough to snag a complementary set of essential tools that every PC gamer should install, one of the many reasons why you should choose PC gaming over consoles .
First, verify your hardware. This is where CPU-Z and GPU-Z come in. From there, you'll want software that collects data by monitoring your PC's sensors so you have a performance record, making it easy to spot irregularities and troubleshoot them. That's exactly what HWiNFO 64 brings to the table, and it can work in tandem with MSI Afterburner's optional RivaTuner install. By combining these two apps, you can display an in-game overlay while benefiting from HWiNFO's more detailed reports.
With the right tools, you can see how your hardware performs, game by game, with live stats. This lets you tune your graphics settings to get the most out of your hardware by using it correctly, improving performance and making the most of your hard-earned money.
Technically, these are two separate tools, but they indeed cover the most important hardware in your PC: your motherboard, CPU, GPU, and RAM. With CPU-Z , you can easily identify your CPU to confirm it is legitimate hardware, and you can also identify your motherboard and RAM. Better yet, the app also shows users their live CPU and memory frequencies, making it easy to see your clock speeds. So you cannot only verify your hardware, but also ensure your components run at their intended settings. Just keep in mind that you can only take snapshots of your hardware info; the app has no live logging despite its live reporting.
Jumping over to GPU-Z , you can use it to verify your GPU, identify the model and its specs, and check your video-memory capacity; you can also view GPU and memory clocks, not to mention temperatures. Watching the app's output will give you an idea of your normal operating conditions, data that will help you troubleshoot should you run into issues when playing your games, perhaps with an overlay that reports your system's stats, which is where the tools HWiNFO 64 and RivaTuner come into play (more about these below). And if you'd prefer to skip unnecessary bloat with as few installed tools as possible, you can even use GPU-Z to log your sensor readings, like if you wish to run the app in the background when gaming, to then pore over your logs when done to see if there were any outlying problems with your performance.
If you want to log as many of your sensors as possible, HWiNFO 64 is the tool to use. It goes well beyond GPU-Z for GPU and video memory, and it also includes reports for your CPU and RAM, all in one app. Better yet, HWiNFO 64 can basically plug into the RivaTuner Statistics Server app (RTSS), greatly expanding its live overlay reports. So not only can you dig into your CPU/GPU temperatures, clock speeds, utilization, power readings, and fan speeds with HWiNFO 64, you can also cross-reference your GPU data with GPU-Z to make sure the reported stats line up.
Your main goal with HWiNFO 64 is to run its logging in the background before you start gaming, say, if you plan to open one of the more demanding titles you want to tame. When a game starts misbehaving, perhaps by skipping a few too many frames, you'll have logs to help narrow down what might be limiting performance, be it your CPU, GPU, or memory. This way, you can better identify which component warrants a closer look.
So not only can HWiNFO 64 help to find any cooling issues with a particular piece of hardware, but since you can plug this info directly into RTSS, you can watch this data in real time with an overlay to get a better idea of what particular parts of a game are making your system buckle, so that you can either tune your game settings to de-stress your system, or figure out which components are worth replacing to bring your rig up to speed for demanding AAA gaming.
MSI Afterburner can not only monitor your hardware, but thanks to the packed-in app RivaTuner Statistics Server , you can display this info in real time with an in-game overlay. You can also use the app to adjust your GPU settings, whether you are using an AMD or Nvidia card. It's handy for those who want to overclock or underclock their GPU, adjust fan speeds and set a custom fan curve. Setting your curve can mean the difference between sitting next to a loud jet engine that overaggressively cools at any sign of heat, and a mostly silent room thanks to the fact that you set a curve that ramps up when your games get demanding. Paired with the RTSS overlay connected to HWiNFO 64's stats, you can watch in real time as your temps rise and your fan speeds change, making it easier to adjust them when you can see how they behave.
Once you've gotten the hang of trial-and-error tuning your fan curve, you can do the same with overclocking and underclocking, testing your new settings for instability in demanding games or GPU benchmarks. All silicon is slightly different, so it's best to tune things yourself, rather than follow someone else's specific settings that may cause your gear to buckle. The goal is to balance performance and stability, and these tools make it easier to monitor and test your changes—essentials every PC gamer should install to keep their gaming PC running smoothly .

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq futures gain as investors buy the dip in the AI trade: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq futures gain as investors buy the dip in the AI trade: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stock futures rebounded on Sunday night as traders cautiously dipped a toe back in following last week's rout in shares linked to the artificial intelligence trend.
Nasdaq-100 futures added 0.4%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures ticked 0.2% higher, or 110 points. S&P 500 futures gained 0.2%.
Stable oil prices early Sunday also lent the equity market some support.
In Asia, Japan's Nikkei 225 lost 1.65%, while the Topix was down 1.12% on Monday. South Korea's Kospi was 1.29% lower, while the small-cap Kosdaq Index fell 0.93%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was up 0.37%.
The S&P 500 lost nearly 2% last week, its biggest weekly decline since late June. The Nasdaq tumbled 4.5%, snapping a four-week winning streak.
Concerns around the health of the AI trade took center stage after CNBC reported, citing sources, that Anthropic's third-quarter revenue totaled $16.8 billion . And while that's up from $11.6 billion in the second quarter, it raised flags among investors about the pace of growth with the AI build-out.
Neocloud stock CoreWeave, which uses large amounts of debt to build data centers that it rents out to tech companies, was at the center of those fears. The AI-linked name plummeted 25% last week — its largest one-week drop since November 2025. Investors in the corporate bond market have started to shun CoreWeave, with the company's credit default swaps reaching distress levels .
It's not just CoreWeave whose moves in the credit market are concerning. Goldman Sachs traders noted Friday: "AI Credit Spreads and hyperscalers specifically are at the widest levels of the year. The last time spreads were nearly this high, the underlying equities were 15% lower."
"The widening across the complex has forced investors to confront what happens as AI spending growth slows. AI Capex has likely peaked and financing, sustainability, and returns on capital have become the debate rather than the next near term earnings revision," they said. "Pessimism is increasing, market breadth is low, and [Friday] we saw the second highest amount of puts traded (right behind June of this year)."
Traders were also keeping a wary eye on oil with ship attacks in the Persian Gulf picking up and Ukraine and Russia trading attacks on energy infrastructure. Ukraine hit an oil terminal in St. Petersburg, Russia on Sunday. Longer-dated oil futures have begun to ratchet higher on expectations energy infrastructure disruptions may last well into 2027.
On Sunday however, Brent and WTI crude futures were both trading a tad lower.
A slew of earnings from major companies such as Meta Platforms and Tesla hit the Street this week with optimism those results will stabilize the market.
Asia-Pacific markets fell Monday, with Japanese stocks leading declines in the region.
Japan's Nikkei 225 lost 1.65%,  while the Topix was down 1.12%.
South Korea's Kospi was 1.29% lower, while the small-cap Kosdaq Index fell 0.93%.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was up 0.37%.
Shares of Australia's Cleanaway Waste Management surged 19.84% on Monday after Swedish private equity firm EQT announced an agreement to acquire the company in a deal valued at about $9.3 billion Australian dollars ($6.5 billion).
Under the agreement, EQT will acquire all outstanding shares of Cleanaway for A$3.095 per share in cash, subject to adjustments for any dividends or other distributions.
The offer represents a 32.1% premium to Cleanaway's closing share price of A$2.37 on Aug. 12, the last full trading day before the company first disclosed a potential transaction.
EQT said it sees opportunities to invest in Cleanaway's infrastructure and improve the performance of its waste management network to meet Australia's evolving waste management needs.
Cleanaway's board unanimously recommended that shareholders vote in favor of the deal, citing the significant premium and certainty of cash consideration, subject to no superior proposal emerging and an independent expert concluding that the transaction is in shareholders' best interests.
Asia-Pacific markets were set for a subdued Monday as investors weighed renewed threats from Iran .
Japan's Nikkei 225 was also set to fall at open, with its Chicago and Osaka futures contracts last at 63,985 and 63,630 respectively, compared with the index's previous close of 65,324.29.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was up 0.29% in early trade. Hong Kong market is closed for a holiday.
A senior Iranian security official said Sunday that Tehran had drawn up a new military response strategy in the event of further U.S.-Israeli strikes, amid reports of multiple attacks on commercial ships in waters surrounding the Arabian Peninsula.
“Iran’s armed forces have prepared a response to any new act of adventurism that would be far more devastating than the 12-day and 40-day wars,” Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said in a post on X.
Correction: This post has been revised to reflect that Hong Kong market is closed for a holiday.
Oil prices fell slightly in early trading Sunday even after Ukraine attacked crude facilities in Russia, while more tankers along the Persian Gulf came under attack as well.
Brent crude slipped 1% to $108.80 per barrel. U.S. oil prices lost 0.2% to $101.18.
Fires broke out at an oil terminal and depot in St. Petersburg after Ukraine launched a massive wave of drone strikes on Sunday, St. Petersburg Gov. Alexander Beglov said in a post. Meanwhile, two tankers were attacked off the coast of Saudi Arabia in the Persian Gulf on Friday, according to incident reports from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre.
For more on the oil market, read our story here.
Nasdaq-100 futures added 0.4%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures ticked 0.2% higher, or 110 points. S&P 500 futures gained 0.2%.

articles.title_orig: Report: Putin wants to discuss Ukraine's future with Trump and Chinese president - without Zelensky
articles.title_zh: Report: Putin wants to discuss Ukraine's future with Trump and Chinese president - without Zelensky
articles.content_orig:
Russian President Vladimir Putin proposed a meeting with US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping next month to discuss ending the Russia-Ukraine war, the Wall Street Journal reported Sunday night, citing people familiar with the discussions.
The talks would not involve Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky , an unprecedented move which would be expected to alarm many European countries, WSJ wrote.
According to the report, the Kremlin suggested the three leaders meet on the sidelines of the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, which takes place Nov. 18 and 19 in Shenzhen, southern China.
Putin first suggested the meeting while speaking to Trump on October 9, in the same conversation in which the two leaders agreed that the US would buy Russian diesel fuel and facilitate its sale, a former Russian intelligence officer told WSJ .
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov confirmed that discussions over a potential meeting were ongoing.
“There is no clear understanding yet regarding the meeting itself or its potential agenda, although all three parties acknowledge the hypothetical possibility of such a meeting taking place,” he told WSJ .
A senior US official told WSJ that Trump hadn't agreed to the meeting but may be receptive to the idea due to his desire to end the war.
This comes as Trump and Zelensky publicly criticize the other's decisions, with Zelensky saying on Saturday that Trump's decision to waive sanctions on Russia and tariffs on its goods days before they were to take effect will embolden Moscow to keep attacking Ukraine, and Trump suggesting that Ukraine needs a new president.
Trump claimed that Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did," in a post on Truth Social earlier on Sunday, calling on the Ukrainian leader to stop attacking Russian diesel refineries.
Neither the White House nor the Chinese Embassy in Washington has commented on the report, but analysts told WSJ that a meeting between Trump, Xi, and Putin could advance Xi's ambitions for China's place in global diplomacy.
“China wants to be seen as the pivot of the great powers, and potentially as a mediator between the US and Russia,” Yun Sun, director of the China program at the Stimson Center, a Washington think tank, told WSJ .
However, Chinese officials have expressed concern that the meeting could overshadow China's role in the region at APEC, according to the report.
People familiar with the discussions told WSJ that Xi is also trying to balance support for Putin and economic ties with Europe. A meeting with Putin and Trump to discuss Ukraine could raise the risk of European backlash.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says
articles.title_zh: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says
articles.content_orig:
The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies has called on the European Union to drop import restrictions on products made from the country, arguing it has been "bundled together" in measures aimed a curbing cheap imports from the likes of China.
Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, told the BBC the recently-imposed tariffs on imported steel to the EU were "unfair" and had been put in place "without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in".
He said he wished to see "at least a carve out" for Ukraine to access the EU market.
A spokesperson for the European Commission said the EU "took into account the difficult situation" of Ukraine when deciding its steel policy.
The trading bloc has recently imposed restrictions on steel imports in an effort to protect steel manufacturers of member nations.
It has capped the amount of steel which can enter the EU tax free at 18.3 million tonnes per year - a 47% reduction from 2024 levels.
There are some country-specific quotas in the policy, but the overall aim is to cut the amount of steel that can be imported due to member nations struggling to compete with cheap imports from the likes of China and Turkey.
Despite a free-trade agreement (FTA) being in place between the EU and Ukraine, the FTA does not stop the EU from introducing separate trade protection measures.
"Ukraine has been bundled together into those measures without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in," Ryzhenkov said, pointing to the war with Russia.
"Access to the European market is crucial for survival," he added. "The restrictive measures that have been put in place by the authorities in the European Union, they don't help.
"I think it's unfair that Ukraine has been treated in the same way as all of the other importers into the European Union."
The Ukraine steel industry estimates steel exports to the EU could ultimately fall by about 50–60%.
The EU said Ukraine's specific steel quota guaranteed exports of the metal, but acknowledged this was at a "level lower than in the past years".
"Despite the war effort, Ukraine remains an important exporter of steel to the EU," a spokesperson said, adding it had "offered compensations" to its largest suppliers, which included Ukraine.
Steel products are a foundation in Ukraine's economy. Before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's national income and a third of its exports. The EU is its top customer.
But the industry has suffered from the continued Russian bombardment.
All of Ukraine's steel mills have been bombed at points since the conflict began in 2022, but Ryzhenkov said strikes had "intensified significantly recently".
At one point in September, there was "no single tonne of steel produced" in Ukraine for the first time in about 150 years, he added.
Almost 800 Metinvest workers have been killed since the war began.
Ryzhenkov said the company had "improved the covered areas" at its mills where workers can shelter during air raids.
"The only thing we can do is to design procedures to keep people safe and just obey those procedures and try to minimise the risks."
"Unfortunately, you cannot cover a whole steel mill to avoid it being damaged."
Ryzhenkov said he expected the coming winter to be "one of the hardest in our history".
"We are in a dire situation when we don't have logistics to access any other market apart from the EU and cutting our available market by 60%, that doesn't help for the industry to survive."
