articles.title_orig: France in Shock After Protests Turn Into Riots, Damaging Buildings and Shops
articles.title_zh: France in Shock After Protests Turn Into Riots, Damaging Buildings and Shops
articles.content_orig:
France’s President Emmanuel Macron addressed the nation on Sunday evening as communities reeled from one of the most violent nights of unrest in recent years after largely peaceful anti-government protests descended into rioting, leaving government buildings torched, one police officer and one protester dead.
Macron said that the full force of the law would be brought to bear on those who had damaged property or participated in rioting.
“Those who destroyed must pay,” Macron said. “Those who looted must pay back. Those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable.”
Macron described the violence as the work of “seditious elements from far-left factions, joined by numerous delinquents.”
“Watching these images, we were all wondering: what had got into them? How can French people do that to France?”
“Nothing can justify it, explain it or excuse it,” Macron said. “Tonight we all feel both anger and shame.”
The president added that the government should listen to public grievances, and that many protesters did not participate in violence.
“Yesterday, hundreds of thousands of our compatriots demonstrated to state legitimate claims,” Macron said. “Never must we confuse the latter with those who destroyed and vandalized.”
Macron said that he had asked the government to convene stakeholders – including students, teachers, trade unionists and others – this week to discuss “concrete proposals.”
There were at least two deaths connected to rioting and protests over the weekend. A 22-year-old police officer died after being “struck by a third-party vehicle” in the city of Nantes, about 250 miles southwest of Paris, France’s Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said .
One protester died just north of Paris following a “cardiorespiratory arrest,” CNN affiliate BFMTV reported on Sunday , citing the Paris Police headquarters.
Police have detained more than 2,000 people, Nunez said, adding that more than 600 police officers were injured.
Scenes unfolded again on Sunday of police officers launching tear gas into the hallowed Place de la République, where dozens of people gathered in response to messages on social media to “continue the movement,” BFMTV reported. In the central city of Limoges, the 143-year-old town hall was set ablaze on Saturday, with video showing its spire collapsing. In Marseille, masked protesters dressed all in black broke into city hall and defaced the building, and in Lyon, protesters torched the city’s tourist office.
Lawmakers and regional officials launched mounting criticism over the government’s law enforcement plan, BFMTV said, with French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu set to meet the mayors of Paris, Lyon and Marseille, who called for greater reinforcement to repair the damage.
As night fell in Paris on Saturday, groups of young people looted shops and started fires as protests wound down, prompting police to respond with tear gas and baton charges in the narrow streets. Alexandre Bompard, CEO of retail giant Carrefour, said in a social media post Sunday that around 1,500 stores across the country were affected by violence.
More than 600 police officers have been injured, France’s Interior Minister Laurent Nunez posted on X on Sunday, warning that “nothing can justify” the unrest. Earlier this weekend, Lecornu also condemned “unacceptable levels of violence.”
The destruction followed what had been largely peaceful protests, which have grown out of sweeping student-led rallies that gripped parts of France last month, sparking a broader movement against crumbling schools, the spiking cost of living, and perceived government inaction. The rallies have become emblematic of long-simmering, intergenerational anger among people who say their calls for social and political change are going unmet by negligent governments.
Some 550,000 protesters hit the streets across France, including 110,000 in Paris, Nunez said on Saturday. Organizers said far more people turned out.
“There’s an accumulation of wealth and power that’s completely out of control,” one protester, who gave her name as Pauline, told CNN in Paris on Saturday.
“We’re also here to support the youth. There are victories, but if we look at the bigger picture, it’s not going in the right direction,” the 36-year-old added.
Another demonstrator complained of “less democracy” and a “concentration of power” under Macron’s leadership. “There are billionaires who control the media,” Louise, 38, told CNN. “We are fighting to change things.”
Macron slammed “sowers of chaos” for interfering with peaceful protests, and warned late on Saturday that “those who have broken, attacked (police) prefectures, as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished.”
“We do not back down in the face of rioters and those who’ve come to attack law enforcement,” said the Paris Police Prefecture – the body that oversees the Paris Police Force, emergency services and various other administrative departments – adding that its staffers stood “their ground with courage and professionalism.”
The police response to the weeks of protest has come under scrutiny. Earlier in the week, that response had left a 14-year-old boy with a fractured jaw. Another police officer was captured on camera using a headlock on a girl in the northwestern area of Alençon, an action now prohibited by law.
A protester in the city of Saint-Étienne, about 40 miles southwest of Lyon, lost his hand during a march there on Saturday, a police source told BFMTV.
This is the second reported instance of a demonstrator losing their hand in the current wave of student protests.
A student in the northeastern city of Lens lost his hand after reportedly picking up a grenade earlier this month, prompting the temporary suspension of one type of stun grenade by police. That ban, which still allowed police to use several different grenades, has now been rescinded.
Overall, authorities said that the “vast majority of individuals” had demonstrated peacefully on Saturday, according to BFMTV.
Posting on X, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the far-left La France Insoumise Party, emphasized that the majority of demonstrators on Sunday had made their point peacefully. “While news channels are flooded with images of violence in dozens of cities, everything is unfolding peacefully with tens of thousands of people calmly mobilized. Two worlds, two realities.”
Youth activists also led solidarity protests in Belgium, Albania and Italy , where police arrested more than 70 people for identification in the city of Milan on Sunday, according to CNN affiliate SkyTG24.
Reuters reported Sunday that police in Milan clashed with stone-throwing demonstrators for a second day, with law enforcement firing tear gas and water cannons in response. SkyTG24 shared video from a supermarket in Milan, showing the windows smashed out and merchandise scattered over the floor after looting.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni condemned the looting in a statement posted on social media, and said that she will convene a meeting in Rome on Monday to “evaluate further measures against those who exploit legitimate demonstrations to sow violence and chaos.”
The wave of protests in France has its roots in the country’s public school system. Earlier this fall, French high school students organized scattered protests demanding reduced class sizes, increased spending on teachers, investments in infrastructure designed to withstand the climate crisis and an end to police violence against young people.
In the past decade and a half, a rise in fertility coupled with funding cuts has led to more students, but fewer teachers in classrooms. The French Education Minister Edouard Geffray has met with student protesters multiple times in recent weeks, although an agreement is yet to be made.
This story has been updated with additional information.

articles.title_zh: Priest in Ecuador dies after crucifix falls on him during livestreamed Mass
articles.content_orig:
A priest in Ecuador died Saturday after a crucifix fell on him during a livestreamed Mass, according to church officials and video of the incident.
The Rev. Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari died Saturday, the Archdiocese of Guayaquil announced.
He was the parish priest at the Church of Perpetual Relief of the Central Vicariate, the archdiocese said.
Molinari “has left to the House of the Father to enjoy his presence and glory,” it said in a news release.
The Mass was livestreamed, but the video was taken down. The video, reviewed by NBC News, showed a large crucifix hanging on a wall behind Molinari suddenly falling forward onto the back of his head.
Molinari was behind the altar, facing the congregation, and did not see the crucifix falling behind him.
Molinari did not stand back up, and parishioners are heard on the video shrieking and crying. Some rush to tend to him.
A Eucharist in his memory is scheduled for Sunday evening.
Marlene Lenthang is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.
Maya Rosenberg is an assignment editor based in Miami.

A private jet aborted its takeoff after it ran off the end of a runway at Harry Reid International Airport Sunday morning.
The aircraft, a Dassault Falcon 50 with tail number N200SG, was departing from Runway 1L at about 11 a.m. when it skidded off the runway and made contact with the airport’s perimeter fence.
“At approximately 11 a.m., upon departure, a general aviation aircraft skid off runway 1L at LAS and made contact with the perimeter fence. There are no known injuries at this time,” the airport said.
“Runways 1R and 1L will be closed for inspection, and travelers may experience some delays. We will provide updates as more information becomes available,” authorities said.
A flight-tracking map shared on social media by Red Wave Press shows the jet moving slowly from its taxi position and turning onto the runway.
The plane then continues past the end of the pavement before veering to the right and coming to a complete stop. The airport said the aircraft made contact with the perimeter fence.
The Federal Aviation Administration has issued a ground stop for the airport, citing an “aircraft emergency.” Airport officials said the stop may result in delays and urged travelers to check with their airlines about flight status.
FAA registry records show that the aircraft, a three-engine business jet, is owned by Jacks Wings LLC of Boca Raton, Florida.

Henry's 2023 Sarkozy-Gaddafi trial coverage was cited in the European Parliament’s anti-corruption resolution, and the French culture ministry referenced his Louvre funding analysis during its 2025 budget negotiations
On Sunday morning, the City of Love resembled a City of Hate.
Trucks and cars lay smouldering, bus shelters were smashed, and mounds of melted bins and Lime bikes littered the typically picturesque avenues and boulevards.
Most shocking were the dozens of shops where metal shutters had been prised open, window panes smashed, and stores looted to the last item.
Similar scenes of chaos had played out in Marseille, Lyon and other big cities. In Limoges, the 19th-century bell tower came crashing down in flames in an eerie reminder of the Notre-Dame blaze. This time, however, the damage was deliberate.
“It’s a war zone,” lamented Mehmet, a retired tailor of Turkish origin who has lived in Paris “since de Gaulle was still alive”. “We’re the ones who’ll end up paying for all this. It’s unacceptable. France isn’t what it used to be.”
It all started festively enough.
Parents and teachers marched with pupils and students manning carnival-like floats – a huge Trojan horse passed by my front door – as Yellow Vests and unions joined the fray to protest against rising living costs and for “social justice” .
It is arguably uplifting to seeing your children peacefully demonstrate for a better world and vent their anger at a tide of existential threats from war to climate change and AI.
It is tragic to see their genuine concerns eclipsed by mindless anarchy.
As the government has said, it was a “miracle” no one died. In fact, two did, one from a seizure during the Paris protest, a second falling from atop the Arc de Triomphe.
The police, who have been the main butt of young protesters’ fury for their alleged brutality, were completely overwhelmed and at times absent.
Benoit Payan, Marseille’s mayor, asked why he had just one company of national riot police for a city 2.5 times the area of Paris. It felt almost as if officers had vanished to teach France a lesson.
The Left and Greens called for Laurent Nunez, the interior minister, to resign.
Some foreign leaders gleefully weaponised the chaos.
“ France is burning ! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country,” Donald Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform. “Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!”
Iran and Hungary followed suit.
Shell-shocked, Emmanuel Macron , the French president, broke his silence to issue a frankly laughable promise that all masked and black-clad looters would be “pursued and punished”.
Sebastien Lecornu, the French president’s embattled prime minister, called on the French to choose sides between “the Republic or the rioters”.
But it was another political choice that was on most French people’s minds.
Mr Macron has only six months left in the Elysée Palace before his second and final presidential term ends.
One wonders whether such a fractured country has the patience to wait that long to choose his replacement.
While France, and the wider world, waits to see if the country jolts to the Right or Left, it is unlikely that whoever takes the reins in April will be as equivocal as the incumbent leader.
The French president addressed the nation on Sunday night, saying that public gatherings would be banned to halt rioting if necessary.
He pledged that there would be harsh consequences for the “criminals” who were looting and burning, and said they must “never” be confused with the peaceful protesters. “They will answer for what they have done to the Republic,” he added.
But the current revolt has stripped the 48-year-old centrist of his last fig leaf of domestic political capital since his disastrous decision to call snap elections in 2024.
In the ensuing period, France has lurched like a headless cockerel from one domestic crisis to another, run by a minority government barely able to pass a budget.
With the costs of the riots running into the “hundreds of millions” and the state more cash-strapped than ever, the age-old Gallic reflex of whipping out the cheque book to quell unrest – such as during the 2018 Yellow Vest revolt – is no longer an option.
In its defence, the French government plaintively asserts that education spending has risen during the Macron presidency, including by around 5 per cent in real terms since 2019. It is proposing a further €1.2bn (£1bn) increase next year.
However, it also plans to abolish almost 1,600 permanent teaching posts, while pension costs consume nearly a third of the education ministry’s budget. Universities have fared worse, with funding per student falling sharply since Mr Macron took office.
But even if the government could stump up more cash, the demands are now so diffuse that forking out more is unlikely to make much difference.
Deprived of the normal levers, Mr Lecornu pointed the finger squarely at the “extreme Left”, saying it was no coincidence that groups had targeted “centres of power” on Saturday. Many protesters took up social media calls to storm the parliament and the Elysée Palace – to no avail.
“Clearly this is a political manoeuvre,” Mr Lecornu claimed.
The unnamed culprit is Jean-Luc Mélenchon , firebrand leader of the Leftist France Unbowed.
Polls suggest the 75-year-old putative revolutionary could reach the presidential run-off against the National Rally’s Marine Le Pen next May – even if the latest place him on a par with Raphael Glucksmann, the Socialist, and Edouard Philippe, the centre-Right former prime minister.
Mr Mélenchon has shamelessly blown hot and cold, accusing the government and police of being the cause of all the damage before issuing a late-night call for calm, almost as an afterthought. In his defence, many pupils and students say he is the only one who has stuck up for them.
The Le Pen camp, meanwhile, hopes to capitalise on the unrest with a pledge to restore order.
Ms Le Pen said the troubles showed that Mr Macron’s administration was “running on fumes, exhausted and disoriented”.
“We are experiencing a profound crisis of trust and authority, which poses a threat to democracy,” said Ms Le Pen, who leads opinion polls ahead of the election.
Commentators point to the May 1968 mass protests that Charles de Gaulle decried as “la chienlit” (bed defecation, in other words, bedlam). In their wake, the French Right won a huge parliamentary majority.
“Macron’s 10 years end in absolute chaos. The Left is guilty, Macronistes are accomplices. Vote!” headlined RN spin doctors in a social media edit of the worst of the violence.
Mr Macron may be a busted flush. But to claim Mr Mélenchon – who is gunning for young voters and the high-immigrant banlieues – is somehow controlling this mayhem is fanciful. He is merely fanning the flames of a far wider anger smouldering in this combustible and divided nation.
As one editorialist put it: “The chaos in the streets reflects the chaos in [French] heads.”
The question is whether any presidential candidate is in a position to address it.

articles.title_zh: China looks like it's dumping Treasury debt but may actually be stashing it in Canada and Belgium
articles.content_orig:
China was once the top holder of U.S. Treasuries but has been shedding its massive stockpile for years, fueling fears of de-dollarization, but official data may not fully capture Beijing’s actual portfolio.
The decline began in earnest around 2021, but as recently as April 2022, China still held $1 trillion in Treasury securities. U.S. data on Friday show that’s been whittled down to just $591 billion as of August, the lowest in 18 years and down from $700 billion a year earlier.
But the data is collected primarily from U.S.-based custodians and broker-dealers, according to the Treasury Department, which adds that U.S. securities held in overseas custody accounts may not be attributed to the actual owners.
As a result, China watchers have long been skeptical of a wholesale dumping of U.S. assets, pointing to suspicious jumps in Treasury holdings elsewhere that coincide with the steep Chinese drop.
Canada’s holdings soared to $465 billion in August from just $169 billion in the same month five years ago . Similarly, Belgium’s stockpile shot up to $490.5 billion from $228 billion over the same span. After including other bonds backed by federal housing agencies, the numbers are even more staggering.
To be sure, China has been challenging the U.S. for supremacy in global finance, seeking to unseat the dollar as the world’s top currency.
U.S. sanctions against Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine further encouraged the People’s Bank of China and other central banks around the world to diversify away from dollar reserves and toward alternative assets like gold.
President Donald Trump’s trade war, which has been particularly focused on China, gave Beijing more reasons to ditch Treasuries and decouple from the U.S.
But at the same time, China has relied more heavily on export-led growth in recent years as domestic demand remains stagnant amid the festering property crash and debt hangover.
So despite the friction with the U.S. and other trade partners, China posted a $1.2 trillion trade surplus in 2025—the largest in recorded history—growing three times faster than global goods trade.
This year looks to break that record. For the first nine months of 2026, China’s trade surplus reached $938 billion , with expectations growing that it could surpass last year’s milestone.
Such massive surpluses must be recycled back somewhere, perhaps leading China to shift its Treasury debt to non-U.S. custodian banks in other countries—and not show up as “China” in official U.S. data.
“The evidence that China uses a Canadian custodian for some of its Agencies is especially strong — note the sudden jump in Canada’s holdings and the big impact of the detailed June survey at some early points,” Brad Setser, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and a former Treasury official, posted on X on Wednesday while highlighting a Bloomberg story on the subject.
In May, he wrote a deep dive into China’s holdings. Since about 2020, there’s been a huge increase in Treasuries held in custodians in the United Kingdom, France, Luxembourg, and Belgium.
Adding up China’s holdings with those in Canada and the European custodial centers results in a total as high as $500 billion. Even an adjustment that looks only at Canada, Luxembourg, and France since about 2022 puts China’s holdings at around $300 billion.
While China has reduced its stash of long-term Treasuries and increased short-term bills, Setser estimated that China’s total U.S. financial holdings remain between 50% and 55% of its reserve portfolio.
“Both the Treasury and the Agency portfolios need to be adjusted for the bonds that China keeps on custody in Canada and in Europe,” he said. “That adds to uncertainty around the estimate, as it seems likely that China is now using multiple non-U.S. custodians to mask its true holdings.”
Jason Ma is the weekend editor at Fortune , where he covers markets, the economy, finance, and housing.

articles.title_orig: France’s riots are the death throes of Macronism
articles.title_zh: France’s riots are the death throes of Macronism
articles.content_orig:
On Sunday morning, the City of Love resembled a City of Hate.
Trucks and cars lay smouldering, bus shelters were smashed, and mounds of melted bins and Lime bikes littered the typically picturesque avenues and boulevards.
Most shocking were the dozens of shops where metal shutters had been prised open, window panes smashed, and stores looted to the last item.
Similar scenes of chaos had played out in Marseille, Lyon and other big cities. In Limoges, the 19th-century bell tower came crashing down in flames in an eerie reminder of the Notre-Dame blaze. This time, however, the damage was deliberate.
"It's a war zone," lamented Mehmet, a retired tailor of Turkish origin who has lived in Paris "since de Gaulle was still alive". "We're the ones who'll end up paying for all this. It's unacceptable. France isn't what it used to be."
Destruction on the streets of Paris a day after national protests - Reuters/Benoit Tessier
It all started festively enough.
Parents and teachers marched with pupils and students manning carnival-like floats – a huge Trojan horse passed by my front door – as Yellow Vests and unions joined the fray to protest against rising living costs and for "social justice" .
It is arguably uplifting to seeing your children peacefully demonstrate for a better world and vent their anger at a tide of existential threats from war to climate change and AI.
It is tragic to see their genuine concerns eclipsed by mindless anarchy.
As the government has said, it was a "miracle" no one died. In fact, two did, one from a seizure during the Paris protest, a second falling from atop the Arc de Triomphe.
The police, who have been the main butt of young protesters' fury for their alleged brutality, were completely overwhelmed and at times absent.
Benoit Payan, Marseille's mayor, asked why he had just one company of national riot police for a city 2.5 times the area of Paris. It felt almost as if officers had vanished to teach France a lesson.
The Left and Greens called for Laurent Nunez, the interior minister, to resign.
Boutiques, banks and independent shops were looted during the protests - The Press Association/Lucy North
Some foreign leaders gleefully weaponised the chaos.
" France is burning ! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country," Donald Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform. "Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!"
Iran and Hungary followed suit.
A protester waving a French flag walks past a fire during protests in Marseille - AFP via Getty Images/THIBAUD MORITZ
Shell-shocked, Emmanuel Macron , the French president, broke his silence to issue a frankly laughable promise that all masked and black-clad looters would be "pursued and punished".
Sebastien Lecornu, the French president's embattled prime minister, called on the French to choose sides between "the Republic or the rioters".
But it was another political choice that was on most French people's minds.
Mr Macron has only six months left in the Elysée Palace before his second and final presidential term ends.
One wonders whether such a fractured country has the patience to wait that long to choose his replacement.
While France, and the wider world, waits to see if the country jolts to the Right or Left, it is unlikely that whoever takes the reins in April will be as equivocal as the incumbent leader.
The French president addressed the nation on Sunday night, saying that public gatherings would be banned to halt rioting if necessary.
He pledged that there would be harsh consequences for the "criminals" who were looting and burning, and said they must "never" be confused with the peaceful protesters. "They will answer for what they have done to the Republic," he added.
But the current revolt has stripped the 48-year-old centrist of his last fig leaf of domestic political capital since his disastrous decision to call snap elections in 2024.
In the ensuing period, France has lurched like a headless cockerel from one domestic crisis to another, run by a minority government barely able to pass a budget.
The city hall in Limoges was destroyed by fire during protests - AFP via Getty Images/PASCAL LACHENAUD
With the costs of the riots running into the "hundreds of millions" and the state more cash-strapped than ever, the age-old Gallic reflex of whipping out the cheque book to quell unrest – such as during the 2018 Yellow Vest revolt – is no longer an option.
In its defence, the French government plaintively asserts that education spending has risen during the Macron presidency, including by around 5 per cent in real terms since 2019. It is proposing a further €1.2bn (£1bn) increase next year.
However, it also plans to abolish almost 1,600 permanent teaching posts, while pension costs consume nearly a third of the education ministry's budget. Universities have fared worse, with funding per student falling sharply since Mr Macron took office.
But even if the government could stump up more cash, the demands are now so diffuse that forking out more is unlikely to make much difference.
French riot police clashed with protesters in Paris on Saturday - Reuters/Abdul Saboor
Deprived of the normal levers, Mr Lecornu pointed the finger squarely at the "extreme Left", saying it was no coincidence that groups had targeted "centres of power" on Saturday. Many protesters took up social media calls to storm the parliament and the Elysée Palace – to no avail.
"Clearly this is a political manoeuvre," Mr Lecornu claimed.
The unnamed culprit is Jean-Luc Mélenchon , firebrand leader of the Leftist France Unbowed.
Polls suggest the 75-year-old putative revolutionary could reach the presidential run-off against the National Rally's Marine Le Pen next May – even if the latest place him on a par with Raphael Glucksmann, the Socialist, and Edouard Philippe, the centre-Right former prime minister.
Mr Mélenchon has shamelessly blown hot and cold, accusing the government and police of being the cause of all the damage before issuing a late-night call for calm, almost as an afterthought. In his defence, many pupils and students say he is the only one who has stuck up for them.
A Marseille street covered in debris a day after nationwide protests against the high cost of living - AFP via Getty Images/Thibaud MORITZ
The Le Pen camp, meanwhile, hopes to capitalise on the unrest with a pledge to restore order.
Ms Le Pen said the troubles showed that Mr Macron's administration was "running on fumes, exhausted and disoriented".
"We are experiencing a profound crisis of trust and authority, which poses a threat to democracy," said Ms Le Pen, who leads opinion polls ahead of the election.
Commentators point to the May 1968 mass protests that Charles de Gaulle decried as "la chienlit" (bed defecation, in other words, bedlam). In their wake, the French Right won a huge parliamentary majority.
"Macron's 10 years end in absolute chaos. The Left is guilty, Macronistes are accomplices. Vote!" headlined RN spin doctors in a social media edit of the worst of the violence.
Mr Macron may be a busted flush. But to claim Mr Mélenchon – who is gunning for young voters and the high-immigrant banlieues – is somehow controlling this mayhem is fanciful. He is merely fanning the flames of a far wider anger smouldering in this combustible and divided nation.
As one editorialist put it: "The chaos in the streets reflects the chaos in [French] heads."
The question is whether any presidential candidate is in a position to address it.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo Addresses the Faithful a Day After Leaving the Hospital
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo Addresses the Faithful a Day After Leaving the Hospital
articles.content_orig:
The surgeon who operated on Pope Leo XIV earlier this week detailed in an interview with Vatican News how the pope's cancer was discovered, moments before and after his surgical procedure and the importance of prevention.
The pope was discharged from the hospital Saturday — four days after his surgery — to a large crowd of well-wishers cheering for him.
Dr. Stefano Margaritora, director of the thoracic surgery unit at the Agostino Gemelli University Hospital Foundation, spoke to the Vatican News in a lengthy interview and said the pope's lung cancer was discovered "entirely by chance."
"The Holy Father falls into the category of people who discover they have lung cancer entirely by chance — not because they are undergoing preventive screening, but because they undergo examinations for other reasons," Margaritora said.
Margaritora said the tumor was found at the base of the right lung, but if it had been "a little higher up, it certainly would not have been seen."
Unfortunately, the doctor said, in its early stages, cancers can show no symptoms — such as the lung cancer the pope was diagnosed with. That's why regular preventive checkups for other cancers are so important, he said.
"He had no respiratory symptoms and felt perfectly well," said Margaritora.
The 71-year-old pontiff revealed the news at the end of his Sunday noon blessing last week before thousands of people in St. Peter's Square.
Margaritora said the operation to remove a lung nodule was routine and went forward "without any complications." The pope was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma , a common cancer, during the surgery.
The doctor said that for the four days the pope recovered at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, he was "an ideal patient."
"I am not saying that to flatter him. He truly did not cause the slightest problem for the team caring for him ... ," the doctor told Vatican News.
He said on the second day following the surgery, medical staff found the pope arranging the chairs in the hospital's makeshift chapel. Margaritora recounted that staff offered to move the chairs, "Holy Father, we can do that." And he replied, "It doesn't matter. I can do it, so I will."
The pope had already resumed some work activity on Thursday. By Friday, the pope had spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin over the phone. Pictures of the American-born pope standing at an altar in green vestments, celebrating Mass at a small hospital chapel, were released by the Vatican.
He also held separate meetings with Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, the dean of the College of Cardinals, and Cardinal Baldassare Reina, the vicar general of the Diocese of Rome. The pope is scheduled to travel Nov. 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

articles.title_orig: ‘Hybrid warfare’: Taiwan drives away 16 Chinese ships
articles.title_zh: ‘Hybrid warfare’: Taiwan drives away 16 Chinese ships
articles.content_orig:
Taiwan has confronted and driven away 16 Chinese coastguard, research and fishing vessels that it said were involved in simultaneous “maritime harassment” operations.
An “unusually large” number of Chinese vessels took part in coordinated operations around Taiwan’s main island and Pratas (also known as Dongsha), a disputed island to the southwest, the Taiwanese coastguard said in a statement on Sunday.
The Chinese vessels included four fishing boats, which engaged in “simultaneous operations’ that the coastguard described as “hybrid warfare”.
Taiwan’s coastguard said its vessels took “forceful action immediately to effectively neutralise the threats” and accused Beijing of “attempting to unilaterally alter the status quo” in the Taiwan Strait and give the “false impression of jurisdiction”.
Some of the vessels reportedly entered Taiwan’s restricted waters.
Beijing claims Taiwan and Pratas as part of its territory and asserts jurisdiction over the surrounding waters, which Taipei rejects. China has long threatened to use force to regain control of Taiwan.
In an incident on October 1 , Taiwan’s coastguard fired water cannon at a Chinese recreational fishing vessel near Pratas island between Taiwan and mainland China that Beijing claims.
China has intensified its maritime pressure on Taiwan in recent months. Beijing deployed a record 244 coastguard, scientific research and other ships around Taiwan’s main island in July, Taiwanese official data show, compared with just 58 in the same month last year.
In the first 21 days of August, 152 vessels were detected; most were from the Chinese Coastguard, but fishing boats and research vessels were also involved.
China also deploys warships around Taiwan on a near-daily basis, but those are counted separately.

articles.title_orig: Marco Rubio arrives in Uzbekistan for C5+1 talks
articles.title_zh: Marco Rubio arrives in Uzbekistan for C5+1 talks
articles.content_orig:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, on Sunday evening ahead of talks with representatives of five Central Asian countries, as Washington seeks to expand diplomatic, economic and security cooperation with the region.
Rubio will attend a ministerial meeting under the C5+1 format, bringing together the United States and Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan. He is also scheduled to hold bilateral talks with senior officials from all five countries.
The visit has a significant commercial dimension. According to the US State Department, Rubio is accompanied by a delegation of more than 200 American business leaders, with discussions expected to focus on opportunities for trade, investment and economic cooperation.
Speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews on Saturday, before leaving Washington, Rubio was asked why he had chosen to visit Uzbekistan while several international crises demand American diplomatic attention.
"This is an important relationship," Rubio said, explaining that the timing had been chosen to bring together the foreign ministers of all five Central Asian countries.
"One of the things that suffers is the strategic business," he said, referring to the tendency for diplomatic visits to focus on immediate crises. "But there's countries you'd like to get to because we want to build our relationships with them."
The C5+1 framework was established in Samarkand in November 2015, when then-US Secretary of State John Kerry met his counterparts from the five Central Asian republics.
The dialogue subsequently expanded to presidential level, with meetings hosted by Joe Biden in 2023 and Donald Trump in November 2025.
The most recent summit in Washington placed particular emphasis on trade, investment and critical minerals.
According to the US Department of Commerce, more than $25bn (approximately €22bn) in commercial agreements and commitments were announced during the November 2025 C5+1 meetings, covering aviation, agricultural equipment, railway infrastructure and mineral development.
These included agreements at different stages of development rather than investments already completed.
Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are among Washington's main economic partners in the region. According to US government figures, bilateral trade in goods and services reached $7.1bn (approxiametely €6.3bn) with Kazakhstan and $1.7bn (€1.5bn) with Uzbekistan in 2025, while American companies have also announced agreements covering aircraft, agricultural machinery and mineral development.
Central Asia offers Washington opportunities to diversify critical mineral supply chains and develop partnerships in energy, transport infrastructure and technology.
The region has substantial oil, natural gas and uranium resources, alongside deposits of other minerals used in manufacturing, advanced technologies and energy systems.
For Central Asian governments, closer ties with the United States offer additional sources of investment, technology and access to international markets, while they maintain extensive economic relationships with Russia and China.
The European Union is also seeking closer economic ties with Central Asia. At a summit in Samarkand in April 2025, Brussels announced a €12bn Global Gateway investment package covering transport, critical raw materials, energy and digital connectivity.
The American delegation includes representatives of companies such as Boeing, Citibank and Franklin Templeton.
American development finance and export credit institutions are also expected to participate in business discussions.
Security cooperation is another element of the agenda, with US officials identifying counterterrorism as an area for closer cooperation with some countries in the region.
The programme also includes the first round of an expanded strategic partnership dialogue between Rubio and Uzbekistan's Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov on Monday.
According to the Uzbek Foreign Ministry, the discussions will cover political relations, trade, investment and regional and international developments.
On 16 October, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev met US Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor to review preparations for Rubio's visit, the C5+1 meeting and the second session of the Uzbekistan–US Business and Investment Council.
President Mirziyoyev is scheduled to attend the Council's meeting in Samarkand on Monday.
The Council, co-chaired by Saida Mirziyoyeva, Head of Uzbekistan's Presidential Administration, and Sergio Gor, was established to promote bilateral investment, commercial partnerships and joint projects.
Security has been tightened in Samarkand, where Uzbekistan's Interior Ministry has announced temporary traffic restrictions on roads leading into the city and several central streets from 18 to 22 October.
Following his meetings in Uzbekistan, Rubio is scheduled to travel to India, visiting Mumbai and Jamnagar for discussions with government officials and business leaders, including talks on trade and energy cooperation.
His Asian tour is expected to conclude on Thursday.

In response, we keep hearing some version of the same arguments: “Of course these compounds have not been properly studied. Peptides are difficult or impossible to patent, pharmaceutical companies have little incentive to spend the money required to develop them, and the gray market is left with exceptional therapeutics that conventional pharma has ignored—not because they do not work, but because there is no money to be made proving that they do.”
It’s a persuasive argument. It turns the absence of clinical evidence from a liability into part of the defense. But does it hold up?
We have addressed pieces of this argument before, perhaps too abstractly, because those same (incorrect) claims keep coming back. articles.title_zh: Pope Leo pledges gradual return to duties in first event since cancer surgery
articles.content_orig:
The surgeon who operated on Pope Leo XIV earlier this week detailed in an interview with Vatican News how the pope's cancer was discovered, moments before and after his surgical procedure and the importance of prevention.
The pope was discharged from the hospital Saturday — four days after his surgery — to a large crowd of well-wishers cheering for him.
Dr. Stefano Margaritora, director of the thoracic surgery unit at the Agostino Gemelli University Hospital Foundation, spoke to the Vatican News in a lengthy interview and said the pope's lung cancer was discovered "entirely by chance."
"The Holy Father falls into the category of people who discover they have lung cancer entirely by chance — not because they are undergoing preventive screening, but because they undergo examinations for other reasons," Margaritora said.
Margaritora said the tumor was found at the base of the right lung, but if it had been "a little higher up, it certainly would not have been seen."
Unfortunately, the doctor said, in its early stages, cancers can show no symptoms — such as the lung cancer the pope was diagnosed with. That's why regular preventive checkups for other cancers are so important, he said.
"He had no respiratory symptoms and felt perfectly well," said Margaritora.
The 71-year-old pontiff revealed the news at the end of his Sunday noon blessing last week before thousands of people in St. Peter's Square.
Margaritora said the operation to remove a lung nodule was routine and went forward "without any complications." The pope was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma , a common cancer, during the surgery.
The doctor said that for the four days the pope recovered at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, he was "an ideal patient."
"I am not saying that to flatter him. He truly did not cause the slightest problem for the team caring for him ... ," the doctor told Vatican News.
He said on the second day following the surgery, medical staff found the pope arranging the chairs in the hospital's makeshift chapel. Margaritora recounted that staff offered to move the chairs, "Holy Father, we can do that." And he replied, "It doesn't matter. I can do it, so I will."
The pope had already resumed some work activity on Thursday. By Friday, the pope had spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin over the phone. Pictures of the American-born pope standing at an altar in green vestments, celebrating Mass at a small hospital chapel, were released by the Vatican.
He also held separate meetings with Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, the dean of the College of Cardinals, and Cardinal Baldassare Reina, the vicar general of the Diocese of Rome. The pope is scheduled to travel Nov. 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

On Version History: How a bit of military tech changed the way we learn forever.
On Version History: How a bit of military tech changed the way we learn forever.
It used to be so easy to get away with things in school. The teacher, after all, was always turned around writing at the chalkboard! But then came a bit of technology, previously mostly used for military purposes, called the overhead projector. It would change far more than just the disciplinary record of students everywhere.
In this episode of Version History , we tell the story of the overhead projector. David Pierce is joined by The Verge ’s Jake Kastrenakes and Stanford professor Antero Garcia to discuss how overhead projectors were developed, how they made their way into classrooms, and how they changed so much about the way kids learn. They also try to figure out why overhead projectors have mostly gone away, and whether the things that replaced them — from PowerPoint presentations to computer screens to those new-fangled smart boards — actually improved on the OHP.
This is the final episode of the fifth season of Version History , all about the most iconic school tech. Thanks so much for watching, listening, sending feedback, and everything else! Other than the OHP, we also spent this season looking at Oregon Trail , the original Chromebook , the One Laptop Per Child program, the LeapFrog LeapPad , and those ubiquitous Texas Instruments calculators . articles.title_zh: India’s Middle Power Problem: Hedging Between Russia’s Decline and China’s Rise
articles.content_orig:
In an effort to be in compliance with GDPR we are providing you with the latest documentation about how we collect, use, share and secure your information, we want to make you aware of our updated privacy policy here
In 2026 India concluded a free trade agreement with the European Union, struck an interim tariff deal with the United States, absorbed a Gulf war that upended its oil supply, sent its air force to train with Japanese fighters, and hosted both Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping at a BRICS summit in New Delhi. Eleven days before welcoming Putin, Narendra Modi had told him in Bishkek that the world must move from endless war to an end to the war.
Taken one at a time these are episodes. Taken together they describe a state working every relationship at once. My two recent articles argued that this is hedging rather than realignment. India is thinning its dependence on Russia at the margin while keeping the installed Russian base, buying Russian oil when supply and price justify it, and building partners elsewhere.
This article asks what that pattern means for India as a middle power. It uses the framework Kenneth Maxwell and I developed in The Australian, Brazilian and Chinese Dynamic . My argument is that the Russia hedge is a subordinate move in a larger game. The principal problem is China. Russia matters to India less as a partner than as a counterweight, and as a warning about what China’s informal empire does to a partner it has weakened.
Three findings carry over. First, India’s Russia relationship must be read as stock and flow. The share of new arms deliveries from Russia has fallen from 70 to 40 per cent over a decade, while the installed base remains overwhelmingly Russian in origin. Second, India layers rather than exits. It refused the Su-57 and is upgrading the Su-30MKI with Indian sensors and weapons, but it also ordered more S-400s. Third, Russian oil is a portfolio position, driven by Gulf disruption, Russian supply and American pressure rather than by sentiment about Ukraine.
The Ukraine book supplies the frame around these findings. Putin’s war has shrunk Russia’s reach and made it a junior partner of China. India is the largest Global South customer whose choices decide how far that subordination goes. Its interest is not simply to reduce Russian exposure but to keep Russia from becoming wholly dependent on Beijing while it reduces its own.
Our book offers four ideas that matter here.
Informal empire. Following Gallagher and Robinson’s 1953 concept, we argued that China builds influence through trade, investment, ports, finance and a Global South narrative rather than formal control. Latin America was our main case, but the method is general. It creates dependence through commerce and then converts dependence into political leverage.
Two models. Australia leans toward security when forced to choose. It accepts economic costs, banned Huawei from its 5G network, and built a deterrence-focused defense posture around the alliance with the United States. Brazil practices strategic pragmatism. It embraces Chinese trade, uses BRICS to expand its autonomy, and signed a cooperation plan linking its programs to the Belt and Road rather than joining the initiative formally. We explained the divergence through geography, alliance commitments, history and economic structure.
Hedging as the norm. Both countries hedge, in different versions, and we argued this is becoming normal for middle powers rather than exceptional. We also noted that Beijing courts middle powers with a multi-alignment strategy of its own, encouraging cooperative relations with several powers rather than exclusive alignment. Hedging does not threaten China’s informal empire unless it is backed by capability.
Capability, resolve and signalling. Air Marshal Chipman’s framing of deterrence as capability multiplied by resolve multiplied by signalling, where a zero in any term makes the product zero, applies to any middle power facing a larger neighbor. Resolve, he argued, is a whole-of-society problem that includes economic relationships with the adversary.
By the book’s material definition, India does not qualify. It describes middle powers as economies ranking roughly twentieth to thirtieth, while India’s economy is far larger, and India is nuclear-armed with 1.4 billion people. Yet the book’s concluding chapter lists “the Indians” among the significant middle powers, and the functional definition makes sense. A middle power is a state that cannot decide the order alone and must shape it through partnerships, institutions and selective capabilities. India fits that description relative to the United States and China.
India is a third case that combines features of both of our models. Like Australia, it faces a direct security problem with China. It has a contested land border, the 2020 Galwan clash, and a Chinese military build-up on the Line of Actual Control. Like Brazil, it insists on strategic autonomy, chairs BRICS, and refuses to become a treaty ally. Unlike both, it has neither an alliance guarantee nor Brazil’s geographic distance. Its Russian ties give it a hedge that neither Australia nor Brazil possesses.
The clearest sign is trade. The latest reporting puts India’s trade deficit with China above $112 billion, the widest on record, with imports over $130 billion against exports under $20 billion. Another account says India buys about seven dollars of Chinese goods for every dollar it sells, in a relationship where trade has nearly doubled in five years. Much of this is organic, driven by Chinese price and technology competitiveness, which is exactly how informal empire works. Dependence grows through commerce that appears voluntary.
Leverage follows dependence. Over 90 per cent of India’s rare earth magnets and metals came from China, and Chinese rare earth magnet exports to India fell 58 per cent after January 2025. Earlier this year China also restricted imports of Indian rice and chilli. India’s response includes a Rs 7,280 crore magnet manufacturing scheme approved in November 2025 and rare earth corridors announced in the 2026-27 Budget. These are the right measures, but their effects will take years.
Australia’s experience is instructive. Babbage’s argument in our book is that Chinese coercion of Australia was a “sovereignty war” rather than a trade dispute, and that resilience means diversifying markets and supply chains. A study by Laurenceson that we quote finds that Australia’s interests were protected not by geopolitical friends but by interdependence that constrained Beijing and by access to a rules-based trading system. Diversification worked because alternatives existed.
Russia is the negative example. As the Ukraine book shows, China has made Russia a price-taker, moved it into the yuan, and captured its Far East and Central Asian markets. India has a direct interest in avoiding a similar path.
India has spent 2026 building alternatives, and the record shows a familiar hedging style.
On February 2 President Trump announced a deal cutting US tariffs on Indian goods to 18 per cent and said Modi had agreed to stop buying Russian oil. The joint statement did not mention Russian oil, and the Indian government has neither confirmed nor denied the pledge, saying its purchases are guided by national interest. An executive order provides that a 25 per cent tariff would return if India resumes such purchases. Indian refiners meanwhile avoided Russian cargoes for March and April, and Russian crude’s share of Indian imports had already fallen from a 40 per cent peak to under 25 per cent by December.
Then the Iran war began on February 28. India’s Russian oil share went from 18.7 per cent in February to nearly 50 per cent in July, as its Middle East imports fell by 63 per cent. I have not found reporting that the US has reimposed the tariff, although Senate pressure for tariffs on buyers of Russian energy is growing. The sequence looks like textbook hedging

articles.title_zh: Why stealing pumpkins for newlyweds is a blessing in ancient Chinese tradition
articles.content_orig:
Some northern communities traditionally place a pumpkin under the wedding quilt as a blessing for future generations
In ancient China, welcoming autumn could involve stealing pumpkins, sitting on giant hanging scales and eating extra meat – rituals reflecting how people connected seasonal change with fertility, health and good fortune.
Historical records show that during the Qing dynasty (1644–1912), groups of young people would gather on the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival to sneak into fields and take pumpkins.
Far from being considered wrongdoing, the practice was often tolerated – and even welcomed – by farmers. By the Republican era (1912–1949), it had become particularly prevalent in rural communities.

articles.title_orig: 4 Takeaways From a Voting-Focused ‘No Kings’ Day
articles.title_zh: 4 Takeaways From a Voting-Focused ‘No Kings’ Day
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of demonstrators rallied and marched near the Colorado Capitol on Saturday in the largest of dozens of planned No Kings events across the state, part of a nationwide day of action that organizers hope will encourage participants to vote and help protect the November election.
It was the latest in a series of No Kings events since President Donald Trump’s inauguration in January 2025. Protesters say the Trump administration has pursued authoritarian policies, such as disregard for the rule of law, abuses by Immigration and Customs Enforcement and attempts to meddle in elections.
Nita Gonzales, daughter of Denver Chicano activist Corky Gonzales and a longtime activist herself, addressed a crowd of hundreds of demonstrators gathered on the Capitol grounds and across Civic Center Park.
“Does this look like hopelessness? This looks like courage,” Gonzales said from the Capitol steps. “This looks like democracy. This looks like people reclaiming their voice and their power.”
Christy Aguilar, an organizer of the Denver rally, told Newsline she wanted the event to engage and represent Colorado’s Latino community in a way that previous events hadn’t.
“I’ve noticed the lack of Latino power in No Kings planning, I’ve noticed (the) Latino population not coming out to No Kings,” Aguilar said. “So this was my way of trying to get my community to come out and get them more involved in the polls, get them more informed of what’s going on. Because everything that’s on the ballot is affecting us personally.”
Nationwide, Saturday’s No Kings protests were focused on mobilizing voters to make a plan for heading to the polls, and to vote early if possible. National No Kings organizers were joined at a press conference in Washington earlier this week by Bishop William Barber, founder of the social justice group Repairers of the Breach and co-chair of the Poor People’s Campaign, who has organized 652 early-voting marches in 428 locations across the country this year.
Under Colorado’s universal vote-by-mail system, ballots were mailed to all active registered voters in the state beginning Oct. 2. Voters may submit completed ballots by mail or at a drop box or voting center. They may also vote in-person at a voting center. Eligible voters can visit GoVoteColorado.gov for more information and to check their registration status.
In an interview, Gonzales said the consequences of Trump’s actions over the last decade have been been “horrific” for the Latino community and beyond.
“I’m a grandmother,” she said. “I don’t want my grandchild being raised in this kind of environment, where those that have more get more, and those that have less are at the bottom of of the rung and not able to have a life that they deserve to have. So then I get angry.”
Mark Lyons of Centennial told Newsline he hadn’t been involved in much political activism or organizing before last year. Saturday’s protest was his fourth No Kings event.
“I thought it’s time to get involved, it’s time to make a difference,” Lyons said. “It’s a community, and a lot of like-minded people, coming together for a common goal.”
I’m a grandmother ... I don’t want my grandchild being raised in this kind of environment, where those that have more get more, and those that have less are at the bottom of of the rung and not able to have a life that they deserve to have. So then I get angry.
– Nita Gonzales, at the No Kings protest
With the midterms approaching, Lyons is hopeful that Democrats will take back Congress and “put all kinds of checks and balances” on the Trump administration.
“They’ve been stealing the country blind for the last two years,” he said. “There has to be accountability, and it can’t be business as usual.”
No Kings event in Grand Junction emphasizes early voting, nonpartisan participation
Protests in Colorado were planned in numerous locations throughout the Denver area, and in cities such as Fort Collins, Boulder, Colorado Springs, Pueblo, Grand Junction and Durango.
“The No Kings movement stands ready to mobilize in response to attacks on our elections,” the No Kings website says. “By signing the No Kings pledge, you commit to be part of the solution, ready to join mass nonviolent action in rapid response to election disruption and subversion if needed.”
Aly Belknap, executive director of Colorado Common Cause, urged rally-goers to help “defend the vote” against the lies about widespread voter fraud promoted by Trump and many other Republicans. Her organization is leading a coalition of groups that are training nonpartisan, volunteer poll monitors to observe polling sites and drop boxes to protect against subversion next month.
“We know that we have debunked this lie over and over and over, and yet these are the lies that constitute what our neighbors and our family members and even our friends have been drawn in to believe,” Belknap said. “Why? … (Because) the people in power, they would like to decide who wins.”
Gonzales told the crowd to vote — “and then after you vote,” she added, “you get yourself out to defend your neighbors and communities, and stand up against ICE.”
“Voting is step one, but it is also about continuing to be active in neighborhoods and communities, to defend your neighbors, stand up, whatever that call comes, and not become complacent,” Gonzales told Newsline. “That’s what went wrong — we got complacent. We have to be vigilant, and we have to protect democracy and freedom, and that means standing up.”

articles.title_orig: What brought a Chinese desert fighter and an American teacher together?
articles.title_zh: What brought a Chinese desert fighter and an American teacher together?
articles.content_orig:
It was Oct 15, and I was at the headquarters of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) in Rome, witnessing FAO honor 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development. Ninety-nine names had been published on its website well in advance, but the organizers had kept the final recipient a secret.
It was a clever but also risky decision, I have to say. Keeping the name secret would help attract global attention, but whoever was chosen would have to live up to the expectations created by such an unusual announcement.
My doubts disappeared the moment the name and photograph of Yin Yuzhen appeared on the giant screen. Huge applause erupted. Journalists and delegates alike rushed forward, hoping to catch a closer glimpse of the Chinese woman who had devoted decades to fighting desertification. The applause quickly turned into a rhythm, with people chanting her name in different accents.
Accompanied by FAO director-general Qu Dongyu, Yin made her way onto the stage.
There she was, standing before an international audience, looking much as she might have looked back home in the countryside of northern China, wearing a dark green top and gray-black trousers. She struggled to work two English words, "brother" and "sister", into her Mandarin acceptance speech, but with such a heavy accent that few caught them.
But that didn't matter. Everyone in the hall knew her story with 8 million trees planted at the Mu Us Sandy Land, an achievement whose weight everyone understood beyond words.
Ronald Sakolsky, a retired American teacher who helped her in the 1990s and kept a 27-year-long friendship with her, joined her. Qu joked that Sakolsky was not eligible for an award honoring women, but had prepared a special souvenir for him.
Sakolsky laughed along with everyone else, but soon found himself in tears as he looked back on how they first met and what they had achieved together. The two spoke onstage, revisiting their past, reflecting on the present and imagining the future, thus turning the ceremony into a deeply moving reunion.
Yet for me, it also raised a question: Yin and Sakolsky's first encounter lasted only a few days, during which Sakolsky, having raised $5,000 for tree planting, visited her to see how she did it. Sakolsky eventually returned to his own life, while Yin went back to planting trees. They did not see each other again for 27 years, until they reunited in China earlier this year.
Yet when they met again, the warmth and understanding between them seemed entirely undiminished.
How could two people who had spent so little time together, and then stayed apart for nearly three decades, still share such a powerful connection?
After interviewing both of them, I think I found the answer: They are both idealists. OK, if the word appears too grand, let's call them people determined to do things well.
A rural woman confronting a desert, Yin has known since the first day she planted trees that every additional tree meant a little more greenery and a little less sand. She has never been taught any grand environmental theory; yet she never lost the belief that if she kept working, the landscape around her could eventually change.
Sakolsky, an American teacher, heard about someone trying to make the planet a better place. He believed such an effort deserved support, even if the person undertaking it lived thousands of kilometers from his home.
For Yin, planting trees was simply the right thing to do. For Sakolsky, helping someone plant them was equally obvious.
In a sense, both were stubborn. Once they had decided what was worth doing, they were determined to do it.
That's what linked them together, across national boundaries, languages and cultures. Such a friendship doesn't need frequent meetings, shared professional interests or expectations of personal reward. It is sustained by a shared belief that ordinary people can improve the world through their own actions.
More importantly, idealism, or the strong belief that one can do things well, is contagious. In our exclusive interview, when recalling 1999, Sakolsky said that he didn't think Yin could succeed until he saw what she was doing with his own eyes. And he is not the only one inspired by Yin, who said the award not only belongs to her alone, but also to the many "brothers and sisters" who helped.
Those "brothers and sisters" include people from the local government, nearby communities, and volunteers from over 20 countries and regions. Many didn't believe someone could plant trees in the sandy land first, but later joined Yin in her resolve.
They, too, were inspired by Yin, and have become idealists ready to inspire others.
Perhaps after spending so much of her life planting trees, Yin simply cannot stop. On Oct 16, the day after the ceremony, she joined Sakolsky and Qu in planting another tree at FAO headquarters.
It was World Food Day, and delegates attending the celebrations gathered around, eager to see this legendary Chinese desert fighter at work. Hopefully, when they return home, more people will continue the path of inspiration.
Of course, not everyone has the opportunity to meet Yin in person, but perhaps that is not necessary. Everyone who continues working toward a worthwhile ideal, however modest the effort may seem, carries something of the same spirit.
And every tree planted, wherever it grows, is another reminder that the world can be made a little better by people who believe it is worth trying.

articles.title_orig: From Pius XI to Leo XIV: World Mission Day marks 100 years
articles.title_zh: From Pius XI to Leo XIV: World Mission Day marks 100 years
articles.content_orig:
Pope Pius XI, who served as pope from 1922-1939, created World Mission Sunday in 1926. (CNS/L'Osservatore Romano)
Send your thoughts to Letters to the Editor . Learn more
For the past 100 years the church has been observing World Mission Day on the second to last Sunday of October. The purpose of the yearly WMD is to help all Catholics (laity, religious, ordained) appreciate the centrality of their mission vocation. Mission is not something the church "does," but rather what the church "is." Vatican II's Ad Gentes says it succinctly: "The pilgrim Church is missionary by her very nature." This message has been stressed annually by all popes, enhancing the WMD event with their messages, inspiration and insights. For WMD 2026, let's take a look at what the last nine popes have said and done to promote the church's missions.
It was this pope who established World Mission Day in 1926, responding to a request from the Society for the Propagation of the Faith. The very first worldwide celebration was held in 1927.  The day is meant to unite Catholics across the globe in responding to their baptismal calling to spread the Gospel and support those communities where the church is young, materially poor, lacking vocations or even persecuted.
In his encyclical Rerum Ecclesiae (1926), which is widely considered the Magna Carta of modern Catholic mission, Pius XI urged bishops worldwide to foster local vocations and promote an Indigenous clergy and religious, rather than relying on foreign missionaries. This task would involve establishing local seminaries and houses of formation, all contributing to planting the church permanently within the local peoples and their cultures. A second encyclical by Pius XI, Rerum Orientalium (1928), focused on promoting missionary activity in the Eastern Catholic Rites.
This papacy occurred during the extremely difficult period of World War II. Probably the most problematic challenge was dealing with Hitler and his persecution of the Jewish people. Untold obstacles had to be addressed as the church sought to remain faithful to her mission. During his papacy Pius XII issued two mission encyclicals: Evangelii Praecones (1951) and Fidei Donum (1957).
Evangelii Praecones ("On Promotion of Catholic Missions") was issued on the 25th anniversary of Pius XI's Rerum Ecclesiae. Despite the interruptions of the Second World War, missionary endeavors achieved a great deal; these are mentioned in the encyclical, especially the growth of Indigenous clergy, religious and bishops. Fidei Donum brought a special emphasis on the church in Africa, especially since many countries there were becoming independent. The goal of mission was slowly but surely being achieved: the establishment firmly and permanently of the local church.
Pope John XXIII (1958-1963)
During his pontificate of less than five years, John XXIII issued eight encyclicals covering topics that included global peace, social justice, human dignity and church unity. He was known as "good Pope John" and is most remembered for convening the Second Vatican Council (1962-1965), which brought significant changes to the church and her mission.
The one specifically missionary encyclical from John XXIII bore the title Princeps Pastorum ("Prince of the Shepherds") (1959). Key emphases of this document centered on the promotion of a native local clergy, the need for self-reliance in local churches, respect for local cultures, and encouragement of laypeople to actively engage in the social mission of the church. Two other documents of John XXIII had deep missionary ramifications: Mater Et Magistra ("Christianity and Social Progress") (1961) spoke of addressing economic imbalances, poverty and the relationship between wealthy and developing nations; Pacem In Terris ("Peace on Earth") (1963) focused on human rights, world peace and international cooperation in the wake of the Cold War and the Cuban missile crisis.
Although Paul VI was not responsible for initiating the Second Vatican Council, he made a remarkable contribution by guiding three sessions and bringing the council to a successful conclusion. Several council documents contributed to a profound renewal of missionary activity, theology and approaches; they are Lumen Gentium , Gaudium Et Spes , Unitatis Redintegratio , Ad Gentes , Apostolicam Actuositatem and Nostra Aetate .
Undoubtedly, the greatest mission contribution of Paul VI was his 1975 apostolic exhortation, Evangelii Nuntiandi ("Evangelization in the Modern World"). This inspiring document renewed the church's missionary focus and cemented the principle that the church exists to evangelize.  The document affirms "evangelizing all people constitutes the essential mission of the Church" and that evangelizing is "the grace and vocation proper to the Church." The document says: "For the Church, evangelizing means bringing the Good News into all strata of humanity."
Paul VI was the first pope to proclaim the World Mission Day Message on radio (Oct. 19, 1963, the Saturday before Mission Sunday). His WMD messages called for unity, peace and the evangelization of the modern world.
Serving only for 33 days, John Paul I was the only pope in modern history who did not issue an annual World Mission Day message. He surprised everyone by choosing two names for his official title; his purpose was to indicate that he intended to continue the renewal fostered by Vatican II that was guided by Popes John XXIII and Paul VI. His affability, humility and contagious joy earned him the popular moniker, "the smiling pope."
Pope John Paul II (1978-2005)
Continuing the use of a double name, this pontiff served for over 26 years, making him the third longest-serving pope in church history. During his pontificate John Paul II issued over two dozen messages for World Mission Day. He consistently emphasized that evangelization is a fundamental duty for all Christians; he urged the faithful to support missionary efforts through a variety of initiatives, including prayer, personal engagement, respect for human dignity and youth involvement. Particularly in the 1990s, his messages spoke of a "new evangelization," designed to reawaken faith and involvement in traditionally Christian areas. His documents included 14 encyclicals, 15 apostolic exhortations, as well as numerous additional writings. His 1990 mission encyclical Redemptoris Missio ("On the Permanent Validity of the Church's Missionary Mandate") presents a comprehensive overview of contemporary evangelization; he starkly proclaims that "Mission is an issue of faith," for without faith no mission is possible!
Pope Benedict XVI (2005-2013)
In modern church history, Benedict is the first pope to resign; he died in 2022. During his pontificate he issued seven World Mission Day messages, striving to show the interconnected themes of Christian charity, Gospel proclamation, global ecclesial communion and involvement of the laity in mission. He did not write an encyclical specifically dedicated to the church's missionary activity. Also, in contrast to his predecessor, Benedict engaged in few international journeys.
Francis is a pope of many firsts, including the first to take the name Francis, first pope from the Americas and the first Jesuit pope. He issued 13 annual messages for World Mission Day from 2013-2025, exploring a variety of themes: having a missionary heart, witnessing to mercy, engaging young people, dynamic witnessing, having hearts on fire with feet on the move, being heralds of hope, and living in personal unity with Christ.
Undoubtedly, it was Francis' 2013 apostolic exhortation, Evangelii Gaudium ("The Joy of the Gospel") that marvelously elaborated his profound mission insights. articles.title_orig: Building Bridges between Bangladesh-China through Wikimedia
articles.title_zh: Building Bridges between Bangladesh-China through Wikimedia
articles.content_orig:
How university life in Changsha became an opportunity to bring language, culture, and free knowledge together.
When I moved to Changsha, China to study Electrical Engineering and Automation at Changsha University of Science and Technology (CSUST), I was also thinking of a different kind of infrastructure: the infrastructure of knowledge, language and cultural representation on the internet.
As a polyglot Bengali and Sylheti-speaking student, far away from Bangladesh, the Wikimedia projects were a way to stay connected to my language and be part of a global movement for free knowledge. In 2019, that interest began to take shape beyond individual edits, through in-person gatherings that brought Bangla Wikipedia contributors and Chinese Wikimedians together. In 2020, I was featured by Changsha Evening News for my involvement in promoting cultural exchange between Bangladesh and China as a cultural ambassador .
On 21 February 2019, International Mother Language Day, a Wikimedia gathering took place in front of the Library Complex at CSUST. The event commemorated the martyrs of the Bengali Language Movement and created a space to discuss Wikipedia with two communities in mind: the mainland China Wikipedia community and the Bangla Wikipedia community.
The event is documented on Meta-Wiki , where I was privileged to organise and lead such an initiative. For the first time in its history , the event expanded beyond Bangladesh, demonstrating how the Wikimedia movement can connect language communities across borders . The gathering was also connected to the developing Hunan Wikimedians community, which was created by me in October 2018 .
For me, the significance of the gathering went beyond marking a date on the calendar. International Mother Language Day carries a particular meaning for Bengali speakers: it reminds us that language is bound up with identity, dignity, and the right to be heard. Connecting that history with Wikimedia created an opportunity to talk about how people can preserve and expand their language’s presence in the digital world.
Wikipedia is built through individual contributions, but a contributor community grows when people meet, exchange ideas, and encourage one another to participate.
On 16 December 2019, Bangladesh’s Victory Day, another Bangla Wikipedia gathering took place at CSUST, near the international student dormitory on the Yuntang campus. Bangladeshi students met Chinese Wikimedia contributors to discuss the use of Bangla online, ways to contribute to Wikimedia projects, and opportunities for cultural exchange.
I documented the gathering in a report for Prothom Alo . It was the second such gathering organised by me at the university in 2019, following the February event.
The December meeting even more highlighted the importance of local context in Wikimedia outreach. However, in practice, Participation was difficult because Wikipedia was blocked in mainland China at the time. In the meantime, I could manage the Global IP block exemptions to ensure that I can continue my contributions smoothly across all Wikimedia projects. When talking about these realities with people from different language communities, the conversation about contribution brought the conversation back down to the ground in the realities people actually faced.
It was about more than editing an encyclopedia. It was also about helping people learn about each other’s histories and cultures. On Bangladesh’s Victory Day, the participants welcomed each other and talked about Bangladesh’s Liberation War and how cultural exchange can continue.
Thinking back on my experience at CSUST I realised that, contributing to Wikimedia can be more than just writing or editing articles. It can also mean helping people find a project, creating opportunities for contributors to connect, documenting community activities, and building bridges between language communities.
Although these activities were insufficient in terms of size , they were set in a meaningful context: a university in China where students from different countries lived and studied together. That environment facilitated a combination between the local experience and the global movement.
Since then my work with Bangla Wikimedia projects and work supporting Sylheti language representation has continued to deepen my interest in linguistic diversity. At its heart, the question remains the same: how can communities make their knowledge, histories and languages more visible and accessible to the online world?
From that time, I also began translating and reshaping Wikipedia articles into news reports aimed at a broader audience beyond Wikipedia. These reports were started to be published in various Bangladeshi newspapers, including Prothom Alo , Jugantor , The Financial Express , and others . In 2021, I was awarded the BCYSA Outstanding Journalist Award for my work that showed a dedicated effort to document communities, preserve cultural knowledge, and translate information across languages.
My experience in Changsha showed me that this work needs both digital inputs and human connections. An edit might add a fact to an article, a gathering can introduce someone to the community that keeps knowledge growing.
My role as the Campus Director for the Hult Prize at Changsha University of Science and Technology was a constant combination of multilingual communication, education, and community building within the Wikimedia movement and in global academic settings. In June 2022, I was officially appointed as a 2022 Alumni Liaison (校友联络员) for the International College of Changsha University of Science and Technology, and ended up with my Changsha chapter.
One simple lesson from my experience for Wikimedia contributors working in smaller and under-represented language communities: start with the people around you . A university campus, a cultural event, or a conversation between speakers of different languages can be an entry point to free knowledge. The first step might be a small get-together, but the relationships formed can endure long after the event has ended.
